questionText: Explain herbicide resistance.
stem: Herbicide resistance confirmed in wild oats. The wild oat is one of the most widely recognised weeds in Ireland's tillage fields. If left unchecked, this predominantly spring‐germinating self‐pollinating weed can substantially reduce crop yields due to its competitiveness. Control of wild oats includes hand‐rogueing, direct drilling, crop rotation and total herbicides. However, some growers report increasing control difficulties when using herbicides. To investigate these reports further, Teagasc collected samples from six wild oat field populations that survived the use of the total herbicide. Teagasc found in all of the six cases the control of wild oats with these total herbicides did not work. This is extremely serious for future control of wild oats on these farms and it is vital to eliminate these weeds, or at least to contain these resistant weeds to the fields where they were found. (Adapted from Farmers Journal, 2020)

rows.verbatim: (Chemical or herbicide) does not kill the (targeted) plant
accepts: inherited ability of a plant to survive and reproduce following exposure to herbicide that would normally be lethal to the plant species
rows.contextNote: One marking point with two accepted wordings — the scheme separates them with a solidus, so either scores the full 2.

notes: Q2 offers a choice of (a) or (b); both routes are carded separately. The scheme's second wording is carried in accepts rather than as the row verbatim only because a marks digit is typeset in the middle of that line in the extraction; the wording is the scheme's own.

The Irish Moiled is one of the rarest Irish cattle breeds. It is a hornless medium sized breed with a mature cow weighing up to 650kg. Traditionally a dairy cow with yields of up to 5000 litres, it has earned the reputation as a truly dual purpose breed. In the suckler herd the cow will go into a negative energy balance to ensure the calf gets the best start in life.
They are generally easy to handle with a placid docile temperament. Surplus males sell well as steers finishing between 20-24 months on good quality forage diet to carcass weights from 220-260kg. The beef is of superb quality with a distinctive flavour.
The cow can be relied upon to produce a calf every 12 months if kept in good health and body condition. They will calve to a continental bull without difficulty and will continue to breed satisfactorily until at least ten years of age.
Tradition has it that they are 'big bellied' to consume and digest large quantities of poorer quality forage which was their traditional diet. They can be termed 'ready browsers' because they will graze willow, ash and ivy, which makes them ideal in extensive or conservation grazing situations.
They are sound in hoof and leg and at home on most types of terrain. They grow a thick winter coat and out-winter happily although being a heavy animal they will poach soft ground.
(Adapted from thecattlesite.com)

stem: Slurry System Technology that Reduces Ammonia Emissions. EASYFIX was awarded the first Green Impact Award for its pioneering technology designed to reduce methane and ammonia emissions from slurry storage at the 2024 National Ploughing Championship. The system injects compressed oxygen into the slurry at specific points via non-return valves. The oxygen that flows through the valve creates a bubble and as it rises through the slurry it helps to break the slurry down and ensures that it remains in a liquid state. The benefit of this technology is that it is proven to reduce ammonia emissions by up to 51%. It also greatly assists in the increased availability of nutrients such as Nitrogen (N), Phosphorus (P) and Potassium (K) in the slurry. The liquid state of the slurry eliminates the need for agitation. (Adapted from enterpriseireland.ie, 2024)
questionText: Briefly explain how the use of this technology could be safer for (1) animals and (2) the environment.

accepts: reduced runoff due to increased nutrient absorption by plants

notes: '4+1' is the SEC ordered split: the first correct answer met scores 4 and the next 1. The paper asks for animals first, so the marks are laid out in that order; a student who answered only the environment point scored 4, not 1.

The report is to assist farmers and their veterinary practitioners to control losses due to liver fluke and pneumonia through capture, analysis and reporting of abattoir data from post mortem meat inspections. Analyse and interpret the report and answer the questions that follow. LIVER SCORES (liver lesions result in reduced performance) — 1 Normal liver: no liver abnormalities detected. 2 Liver damage by fluke but no live fluke: fluke may not be observed because the animal was (i) treated and cured, (ii) has undergone 'self‐cure' or (iii) live fluke may have been present but not observed. 3 Liver damage by fluke and live fluke: fluke may be present because the animal was (i) not treated, (ii) re‐infected after a previous treatment, (iii) treated with a product that only kills adult fluke leaving young fluke alive, (iv) given a product to which the fluke have become resistant. 4 Liver other: liver damage due to other causes, e.g. tumours. 5 Liver abscess: may occur following gut damage from a high grain diet or as an infection from a 'navel ill' or other infection. LUNG SCORES (lung lesions result in reduced performance) — 1 Normal lung: no lung abnormalities detected. 2 Limited lung damage as a result of pneumonia (viral / bacterial infection). 3 Extensive lung damage as a result of pneumonia (viral / bacterial infection). 4 Lung other: lung damage due to other causes, e.g. abscess or tumour. THE REPORT — Tag | Sex | Age (months) | Carcase (kg) | Liver Score | Lung Score: IE 1234567-8-0001 | E | 20 | 330 | 1 | 3 · IE 1234567-8-0002 | C | 22 | 360 | 3 / 5 | 1 · IE 1234567-8-0003 | D | 40 | 400 | 2 | 1 · IE 1234567-8-0004 | B | 44 | 500 | 1 | 2 · IE 1234567-8-0005 | E | 19 | 340 | 3 | 1 · IE 1234567-8-0006 | C | 20 | 350 | 2 | 4 · IE 1234567-8-0007 | D | 56 | 410 | 4 | 1. Sex key: A = young bull, B = bull, C = steer, D = cow, E = heifer. (Adapted from Animal Health Ireland, 2019)

rows.verbatim: Conclusion: animal has liver damage due to fluke being present in the past or live fluke present and; Not treated (misdiagnosed) ‐ the animal was not given an anthelmintic (dose / drench) to treat the parasitic load
rows.contextNote: ONE conclusion is asked for. The scheme's opening clause — liver damage due to fluke in the past or live fluke present — is common to every route; the accepts list carries the other endings the scheme allows after it.

Treated with product that only kills adult fluke leaving the immature fluke to survive and mature causing liver damage

stem: An investigation looking at milk production from grass and white clover systems over the course of a year was carried out by Teagasc researchers in Moorepark. stem: Lisa wanted to sow a food crop in a two hectare field in an environmentally friendly way. Using a food crop (other than grass) you have studied, answer the questions which follow. Question 14 is 50 marks, made up of parts (a) and (b) with no choice.
questionText: Briefly outline two factors which affect the preservation of the crop.

rows.verbatim: Temperature or light
rows.contextNote: Naming a factor is worth 2 marks; the scheme allots 2(2) to the two factors and 2(1) to the two outlines.

rows.verbatim: moisture
rows.contextNote: A second, different factor.

rows.verbatim: Temperature – if temperature is too warm crop can overheat or respire causing spoiling of the crop
accepts: pH – if pH is not suitable grain may sprout in storage or grain may rot
Oxygen – foods store best with no oxygen or the presence of oxygen may speed up spoilage
rows.contextNote: The outline of the first factor is worth 1 mark, and it must match the factor named above. The scheme also credits the cold side of the same point and the light option: 'too cold frost damage can occur or light will cause potatoes to sprout or turn green'.

rows.verbatim: Moisture – crops last longer when moisture is removed (e.g. reducing moisture in cereal crops)
accepts: pH – if pH is not suitable grain may sprout in storage or grain may rot
Oxygen – foods store best with no oxygen or the presence of oxygen may speed up spoilage
rows.contextNote: The outline of the second factor, worth 1 mark, matched to the factor named above.

notes: The scheme prints two tariffs side by side for this part: 'Factors- 2(2)' and 'Outline- 2(1)', i.e. two factors at 2 marks each plus two outlines at 1 mark each = 6, which is what Q14(a) needs to reach 22. Four rows therefore: two factor rows at 2 and two outline rows at 1. The scheme's factor pool is 'Temperature or light / pH / oxygen / moisture' — temperature and light are ONE pool entry joined by 'or', so they are one row, not two. The scheme's line 'Outline of factor:' is a heading with no answer in it and is deliberately not transcribed (LAW 3). The light option and the 'too cold' half of the temperature outline run across the marks column in the extraction (lines 552-554) and so cannot be quoted as verbatims. Filed under crop harvesting because the scheme's outlines are all about storage of the harvested crop.

stem: Lisa wanted to sow a food crop in a two hectare field in an environmentally friendly way. Using a food crop (other than grass) you have studied, answer the questions which follow. Question 14 is 50 marks, made up of parts (a) and (b) with no choice.

notes: The scheme prints '2(5)', which by its own front matter (p.3) means two parts to the answer at 5 marks each = 10. That is also what Q15 needs: (a) 10 + 10 + 6 + 6 + 6 + 2 = 40 plus 10 for either (b) or (c) = 50. Nine sampling points are printed in one pool and two are claimable, so two rows plus accepts. This part is carded because the two answers are figures a student either knows or does not: the chart is the medium the answer is written in, not information that has to be read off the page, so the card stands without it once the stem states which bars are already drawn (verified by rendering paper p.28: mineral matter 45%, air 25%, the other two blank). Tariff 6+4 is an ordered split by the scheme's front matter (p.4) — the first correct answer encountered scores 6 — so neither row carries a mark value. Topic follows the shipped agsci-2024-ol-q7b, which files ideal soil composition under the soil's physical properties.

stem: Pat is doing a screening on his dairy herd. Based on the results of his investigation, he noticed that the total bacterial count (TBC) had increased.
questionText: Outline ways Pat could reduce the number of bacteria entering the milk.

rows.verbatim: Teat dipping pre and post milking
rows.contextNote: Two ways score, 6 marks each. The scheme prints ten and any two of them earn full marks, so anything in this list is worth the same as the row itself.
accepts: clean housing or clean lying area

rows.verbatim: milk socks or filtering
accepts: Teat dipping pre and post milking
clean housing or clean lying area

notes: The scheme tariffs this 6+6 — two ways at 6 marks each, equal in value, so it is a fixed tariff and not an ordered split. Ten ways are printed and only two may be claimed, so two rows carry the first two and all ten ride in accepts on both, following the deck's established handling of over-long pools (2021 HL Q7(c)). "clip hair on cow’s tails" straddles the typeset 6+6 marks cell in the extraction so it cannot be a quoted row, but it is fully creditable and is carried as an accept on both rows — the same treatment marks-interrupted pool items get on Q17(a)(i), Q17(a)(ii) and Q18(c)(ii). Not an open list — the scheme's pool does not end in "or any other" — which is exactly why every one of the ten had to be reachable.

stem: Pat is doing a screening on his dairy herd. He wanted to check the quality of a milk sample. In part (i) you described the investigation he would carry out — the resazurin test, or a total bacterial count by serial dilution.
questionText: Identify the following variables in the investigation in part (i): Independent, Dependent, Control.

rows.verbatim: Independent — Milk sample
Dependent — Quality – colour change of resazurin
rows.contextNote: One dependent variable, answerable either way: colour change if you ran the resazurin test, colony-forming units if you ran the bacterial count. The solidus is alternative wordings of the same point, not two points.

rows.verbatim: Control — Fresh milk sample or milk sample of known quality or equal volumes of milk
rows.contextNote: Any one valid control scores the 2 marks — the scheme's list closes with "any other valid control variable".

notes: 3(2) = three marking points at 2 marks each, total 6. One row per variable, which is exactly the three rows the paper's table asks for, so the tariff is fixed and not a best-of. Inside the Dependent and Control cells the solidi separate alternative wordings of one answer, so they are accepts and not extra rows. The extraction interleaves the scheme's label column with its answer column, so each verbatim quotes the contiguous span only and the label is prefixed with an em dash; the Control pool in full reads "Fresh milk sample or milk sample of known quality or equal volumes of milk or equal volumes of Resazurin or all test tubes sterile or any other valid control variable".

stem: Pat is doing a screening on his dairy herd. In part (i) you described the investigation — the resazurin test, or a total bacterial count (TBC) by serial dilution. The paper prints two answer lines, headed "Data type:" and "Reason:".

rows.verbatim: Resazurin test – qualitative

The table is numeric data printed as text on the paper, so it is reproduced in the stem and the part is answerable without the figure, the same treatment the deck already gives 2022 HL Q7(b) and 2022 OL Q9(a). The scheme's concession for an unworked correct answer is carried on row 2 rather than modelled as a third row, because it is not a separate marking point.

stem: The paper prints an article, "Irish-based ration achieves 47% reduction in emissions": a large portion of dairy rations fed to cattle on Irish farms are made using ingredients from outside of Ireland and the European Union (EU). Because of this, the emissions associated with these rations are quite high, and these contribute towards overall farm emissions. The farm is focused on becoming the first climate-neutral dairy farm, with a wide range of measures being used to achieve this target. One of the measures used on the farm is the feeding of a concentrate ration made from Irish sources. The ration fed to cows on the Shinagh demonstration farm is made from Irish oats (33%), Irish beans (33%) and Irish barley (34%). (Adapted from Agriland, 2022.) The underlined term is "climate-neutral dairy farm".
questionText: Explain the underlined term, climate-neutral dairy farm.

rows.verbatim: the carbon used = the carbon saved or a balanced carbon footprint
accepts: The amount of greenhouse gas emissions a farm produces is balanced by absorbing or removing equivalent emissions in the atmosphere
rows.contextNote: One 2-mark explanation, offered three ways by the scheme. The full first wording is "The amount of greenhouse gas emissions a farm produces is balanced by absorbing or removing equivalent emissions in the atmosphere" — the typeset 2 falls inside it in the extraction, so the contiguous alternative is quoted as the row and the long form sits in accepts.

notes: A flat 2-mark explanation. The solidi separate alternative wordings of one point, so this is one row with accepts and never three rows. openList is set because the scheme closes the pool with "or valid explanation". The underlined term is confirmed from the PDF's own underline rule beneath "climate-neutral dairy farm" on page 31.

stem: The paper prints an article, "DNA evidence proves Welsh farmer stole neighbour's cow": a farmer in Wales was fined £4,000 after DNA evidence was used to prove he had stolen his neighbour's cow, police have said. stem: Jack used an Artificial Intelligence (AI) app on his phone to research silage making and found the following information. Analyse the paragraph and answer the questions that follow. Jack's prompt: Tell me how to make silage in Ireland. Response given by AI app: "Silage making in Ireland involves a controlled fermentation process that preserves grass and other green fodder for livestock feed. After cutting, the forage is wilted to reduce its moisture content before being compacted and sealed in airtight conditions, such as in a silo, pit, or bale. The presence of oxygen allows anaerobic bacteria, primarily lactic acid bacteria, to ferment the plant sugars, producing butyric acid. This acidification raises the pH, inhibiting harmful microbes and preserving the feed's nutritional value. Silage is a key component of Ireland's livestock farming, ensuring a reliable food source throughout the winter months."
questionText: Identify two inaccurate pieces of information from the paragraph above.

rows.verbatim: Presence of oxygen allows anaerobic bacteria
rows.contextNote: The scheme prints three errors and only two are asked for, under a 4+2 split - whichever correct error the examiner meets first takes the 4.

accepts: Presence of oxygen allows anaerobic bacteria

notes: The AI paragraph is prose printed in the paper and is reproduced in full in the stem, so no figure is needed. Three errors are printed, two are claimable, so the card shows two rows with the remaining errors in accepts rather than three rows that would overstate the tariff. 4+2 = 6.

REVIEWER NOTE: the scheme prints this statement across two lines with the marks cell ('3') landing between 'stick' and 'together', so the sentence is not contiguous in the extracted source. The row keeps every word of the scheme in order and replaces the scheme's comma with an em dash at that break — the same 'clue — answer' form the existing agsci cards use, and the form both gates check against. Nothing is added or removed.

stem:
Flocculation occurs in soils.

Part (ii) set out the steps of an investigation showing that flocculation had occurred in a soil: clay soil is added to two test tubes; calcium carbonate is added to one of the test tubes; water is added to each test tube, which are then stoppered and shaken; they are left to settle, and one test tube stays muddy while one test tube goes clear.
questionText: Identify one control variable used in the investigation shown in part (ii) above.

rows.verbatim: Same amount of soil (clay) or water
accepts: type of soil (clay) used in each test tube
shaken for same amount of time
rows.contextNote: Only ONE control variable is asked for and the whole 3 marks ride on it; the three wordings the scheme prints are alternatives, not three separate points.

notes: Part (ii) itself is skipped (its answer is the letter order D-A-B-C against four photographed boxes), but its four steps are printed as text in the paper and are reproduced in this card's stem, so the card stands alone with no dangling reference. Single 3-mark answer, one row, alternatives in accepts.

stem:
Flocculation occurs in soils.

Part (ii) set out the steps of an investigation showing that flocculation had occurred in a soil: clay soil is added to two test tubes; calcium carbonate is added to one of the test tubes; water is added to each test tube, which are then stoppered and shaken; they are left to settle, and one test tube stays muddy while one test tube goes clear.
questionText: State if the results of the investigation in part (ii) above are qualitative or quantitative.

rows.verbatim: Qualitative

notes: One word, 3 marks, one row — the scheme prints 'Qualitative 3' and nothing else. The result is an observed colour/clarity change with nothing measured, which is why it is qualitative; that reasoning is not in the scheme so it is not put on the row. The investigation is carried in the stem from the paper's own printed steps, so 'part (ii) above' does not dangle.

stem:
Answer both (a) and (b) with either (c) or (d).

Good soil conditions are important for crop production.

List of minerals provided: Nitrogen · Phosphorus · Calcium · Magnesium.
questionText: Four descriptions of plant nutrient functions are given below. Using the list of minerals provided, match each mineral to its correct description. Descriptions: 1. Involved in chlorophyll production; 2. Production of amino acids, which produce proteins for growth and repair in plants; 3. Seed formation and development; 4. Cell wall formation.

rows.verbatim: Involved in chlorophyll production — Magnesium
Production of amino acids, which produce proteins for growth and repair in plants — Nitrogen
Seed formation and development — Phosphorus
Cell wall formation — Calcium

notes: Q17 offers (c) OR (d); (d) is skipped (see the skip list). The scheme prints '5+5+1+1' against the four-row table, so the value depends on HOW MANY matches are right, not which: the first two correct score 5 each and the remaining two score 1 each. That is an ordered split, so every row's marks are null — a per-row number here would be invented. Rows use the 'description — mineral' form; the description is the paper's own table text and the mineral is what the scheme prints. Filed under soil chemical properties, which is where the major elements and their roles are taught, although the descriptions themselves are plant functions.

stem: Aaron wanted to improve the calving rate on his suckler beef farm. He learned that body condition score (BCS) has an effect on cows going in calf and calving period. [The words underlined on the paper are: body condition score]
questionText: Explain the underlined term.

rows.verbatim: The ratio of lean meat to fat on the animal’s body
accepts: a system use to determine the amount of fat on an animal
rows.contextNote: One explanation is asked for and it carries all 3 marks; the scheme's three wordings are alternatives, not three points.

notes: The paper's table of BCS against conception rate is not needed for this part — it is a definition. Single 3-mark answer, one row with the scheme's alternatives in accepts. The scale wording ('1= extremely thin 5 (9) = extremely fat') is carried as an accept because the scheme prints it after a solidus as another way of explaining the term (it reads non-contiguously in the extraction only because the marks cell '3' lands inside it). REVIEWER CORRECTION: the underline on the paper covers the words 'body condition score' only — checked against the PDF's underline rule and word boxes — so the stem no longer claims '(BCS)' is underlined.

stem:
Aaron wanted to improve the calving rate on his suckler beef farm. He learned that body condition score (BCS) has an effect on cows going in calf and calving period. Analyse the table below and answer the questions that follow.

Body condition score (BCS) / % of cows that went in calf at first service / Expected calving period
1 / 35 / 24 weeks
2 / 55 / 12 weeks
3 / 70 / 9 weeks
4 / 65 / 12 weeks
5 / 50 / 15 weeks
questionText: Using the information in the table above, identify which BCS gives the highest % of cows going in calf at first service.

rows.verbatim: BCS: 3

notes: The table is printed as a plain data table in the paper and every value extracted cleanly, so it is reproduced in the stem and the card carries no dangling reference to a figure. Single answer worth the whole 5-mark tariff.

stem: Aaron wanted to improve the calving rate on his suckler beef farm. He learned that body condition score (BCS) has an effect on cows going in calf and calving period.
questionText: Outline two advantages of having a shorter calving period for his suckler herd.

rows.verbatim: More efficient management (if most calves born in a short window)
accepts: all calves at same stage of feeding
efficient labour (for tasks such as vaccinations or dosing)
more efficient breeding programme (for getting cows back in calf)
calves reach growth targets in similar time frame (for slaughter or breeding)
rows.contextNote: Two advantages are required, each worth 2, so there is no order effect. Any two different advantages from the scheme's list of five score.

rows.verbatim: all calves at same stage of feeding
accepts: More efficient management (if most calves born in a short window)
efficient labour (for tasks such as vaccinations or dosing)
more efficient breeding programme (for getting cows back in calf)
calves reach growth targets in similar time frame (for slaughter or breeding)
rows.contextNote: Your second correct advantage, whichever it was, also scores 2.

notes: Tariff '2+2' = 4. Five-item pool, two equal answer slots. 'more efficient breeding programme (for getting cows back in calf)' sits only in accepts because the extracted scheme line breaks it across the '2+2' marks cell; both seeded verbatims are contiguous in the scheme.

stem: Question 18, part (b). Aaron wants each cow on his farm to have one calf every 12 months.
questionText: Calculate X, the window of time available to Aaron to get his cows in calf again, using the following data: 285 day gestation + X = 365 days.
notes: The 'data below' is a one-line arithmetic strip (285 day gestation + X = 365 days) whose every term extracted as text, so it is reproduced in the stem rather than treated as a figure. The scheme adds '(2m for correct method and incorrect answer / correct answer 4m)' — that is a marking instruction, not an answer, so it is NOT a row: if you set the subtraction up right but slipped on the arithmetic, half the marks were still yours.

stem: Aaron wants each cow on his farm to have one calf every 12 months. The timeline below shows a calendar year for a spring calving suckler herd, running Feb, Mar, Apr, May, Jun, Jul, Aug, Sep, Oct, Nov, Dec, Jan, Feb, with Calving marked at each end. The events to place are: A Drying off · B Weaning off · C Mating.
questionText: Insert the letters A, B and C on the timeline below to indicate when each of the following events take place for a spring calving suckler cow.

rows.verbatim: C – mating: April- May
B – weaning off: July
A – drying off: December

notes: REVIEWER NOTE: this is a mark-the-timeline part, but nothing here dangles. The paper prints the legend as text (A Drying off, B Weaning off, C Mating — confirmed against the PDF's own layout coordinates, and the scheme's own rows agree), and the timeline is just the twelve months, which are reproduced in the stem. So the card is answerable in words: name the month for each event. Tariff '4+4+1' = 9 and is positional — the first two correct placements score 4 each and the third scores 1 — so every row's marks are null.

stem: Aaron wants each cow on his farm to have one calf every 12 months.
questionText: Draw a labelled diagram of the leader follower grazing system that is often used on suckler farms.

rows.verbatim: 2 separate fields indicated
accepts: younger animals separated from older animals
rows.contextNote: '5+4': the FIRST correct feature scores 5 and the second scores 4 — the 5 is not tied to drawing two fields. The scheme adds '(Points can be indicated in text)', so a labelled sketch is not the only way to score.

rows.verbatim: younger animals separated from older animals
rows.contextNote: Your second correct feature, whichever it was, scores 4.

notes: No figure needed — the diagram is the student's to draw. Tariff '5+4' = 9 for two credited features, while the scheme lists four possible features, so this is modelled as two answer slots with the full four-item pool in accepts. The scheme's bracketed '(Points can be indicated in text)' is an instruction to the examiner, not a marking point, so it is carried in a contextNote rather than transcribed as a row.

stem: Irish butter is made from milk from grass fed cows.
questionText: Irish butter is made from milk from grass fed cows. Describe two characteristics of butter or another dairy product based on a grass-fed diet.

rows.verbatim: Yellow (due to carotene in grass)
accepts: higher in Vitamin A or D or E or anti-oxidants
rows.contextNote: Two characteristics are required, each worth 2, so there is no order effect. Any two different characteristics from the scheme's list of five score.

rows.verbatim: high in omega 3 or omega 6
accepts: higher in Vitamin A or D or E or anti-oxidants
rows.contextNote: Your second correct characteristic, whichever it was, also scores 2. Note that 'higher in Vitamin A or D or E or anti-oxidants' is ONE point with four wordings — any one of them scores it, and naming two of them does not score twice.

notes: Q18(c)(i) and (c)(ii) are skipped: both are read off the Bord Bia dairy-exports bar chart. This part is a knowledge question about grass-fed produce and needs no graph, so the stem carries only the sentence the paper prints above it. Tariff '2+2' = 4, five-point pool, two equal answer slots. REVIEWER CORRECTION: row 2 previously seeded a TRUNCATED point ('higher in Vitamin A or D or E', cut before 'or anti-oxidants') and listed 'anti-oxidants' as a separate accept, which showed a half point as a row headline. Row 2 now seeds 'high in omega 3 or omega 6', a complete point contiguous in the scheme, and both rows carry the same four-item pool with the Vitamin/anti-oxidant point reassembled whole — it reads non-contiguously in the extraction only because the '2+2' marks cell falls inside that line.

questionText: Outline one disadvantage of using machine (method) B when feeding high producing animals.
stem: Question 3(b) continued, and the last part of the question. Machine (method) B is the implement arrowed in the right-hand photograph at part (b)(i) — the high-sided wagon with the yellow pick-up head, filled with cut grass, working a green pasture. "High producing animals" means stock at peak output, such as a dairy cow in early lactation. This part carries 2 marks.

labelKey.meaning: the red arrow in the left-hand photograph, pointing down at the wide orange hopper-and-tine implement behind a tracked tractor on cultivated ground; printed on the same crop but asked about at part (iii), not here

the red arrow in the right-hand photograph, pointing down at the high-sided trailer loaded with cut green grass, with a yellow pick-up head slung at its front, drawn behind a tractor across green pasture; this is the machine this part asks about

rows.verbatim: Stressed animals due to too much confinement (leading to reduced animal performance) / spoiling of cut grass ‐ reduced intake / increased labour required to feed animals
rows.contextNote: One 2-mark point with seven alternative wordings across the scheme's block. The question asks for one disadvantage, so one wording earns the full 2 and further ones add nothing.
accepts: increased capital investment on housing for animals
increased slurry storage requirement as animals housed all year round

notes: Bound to the inspected crop agricultural-science-2021-HL-paper-p07-i0.png, the same figure as part (b)(i): the paper never names machine B in words, so without the photograph this part asks about an unidentified method. Verbatim stops before the point where the scheme's marks column interrupts the block; the four wordings on the far side of it are carried in accepts. One row, not seven — the scheme prints a single 2 for the whole list.

questionText: Identify each of the following plants commonly found in grassland.
stem: Question 1 offers a choice of (a) or (b); this is part (b). Four colour photographs of plants commonly found in grassland are printed in a two-by-two grid, each with a bold letter above it: A top left, B top right, C bottom left, D bottom right. The letters carry across to part (b)(ii), which asks for a method of killing plant B.

labelKey.meaning: the top-left photograph — a dense grass sward studded with many small flowers with white petals and yellow centres: daisy
the top-right photograph — a low rosette of broad, oval, red-veined leaves growing in rough grass: dock leaf
the bottom-left photograph — a single glossy yellow five-petalled flower among deeply lobed green leaves: buttercup
the bottom-right photograph — a flat rosette of spiny, blue-green, deeply cut leaves lying in grass: thistle

rows.verbatim: A = Daisy
B = Dock leaf
C = Buttercup
D = Thistle

notes: Figure opened and verified. agricultural-science-2021-OL-paper-p04-i0 IS the Q1(b)(i) grid: the 'Or' line, the instruction, then A (a sward of small white daisies), B (a rosette of broad red-veined dock leaves), C (one yellow buttercup flower among lobed leaves) and D (a spiny thistle rosette), ending at the 'A:' answer box — nothing truncated. Pure photograph identification, so the card is meaningless without the crop. The scheme prints 2 beside each of A–D, giving a fixed 8; Q1(b)(ii) takes the remaining 2 of Q1's 10. A surplus wrong name written beside a correct one cancels that letter's mark (see the scheme's own worked example on surplus answers).

questionText: Describe one method used to kill plant B.
stem: Question 1 offers a choice of (a) or (b); this is part (b)(ii). Part (b)(i) printed four photographs of grassland plants lettered A to D and asked you to name them. Plant B is the one in the top-right photograph — the broad-leaved rosette growing in rough grass.

labelKey.meaning: the top-left photograph — a grass sward studded with small white, yellow-centred flowers: daisy
the top-right photograph — a rosette of broad, oval, red-veined leaves: dock leaf. This is the plant this part asks you to kill.
the bottom-left photograph — a yellow five-petalled flower among lobed leaves: buttercup
the bottom-right photograph — a spiny, deeply cut rosette in grass: thistle

rows.verbatim: Spray (with herbicide or weed killer)
accepts: digging up or ploughing (to remove weeds)
crop rotation to disturb (break) weed cycle
rows.contextNote: The solidi separate three wordings of ONE 2-mark point, not three marks. Only one method is asked for and it carries the whole 2.

notes: Figure opened and verified — the same Q1(b)(i) crop, bound because 'plant B' is a dangling reference without it. The card does not hand over the identification: the scheme's methods (spray, dig/plough, rotation) score for any broad-leaved weed, and B is decoded only in the label key, which renders after the reveal. Solidus discipline: three alternatives, one mark point.

questionText: Identify the labelled parts A, B, C on the diagram using the correct word from the list.
stem: Question 2 prints a diagram of part of the digestive system of a sheep, with a photograph of grazing ewes beside it. Three chambers are lettered A, B and C; the oesophagus, the reticulum and the small intestine are already named on the diagram itself. The word list printed under the diagram is: Omasum, Rumen, Abomasum — three words for three letters, so every word is used once. Part (b) then asks for two functions of the microorganisms in a ruminant's digestive system.

labelKey.meaning: the arrow entering the large rounded chamber that fills the right-hand half of the diagram — the rumen, the biggest compartment
the arrow pointing up into the chamber at the bottom centre of the diagram — the abomasum, the true stomach
the leader pointing into the chamber in the middle of the diagram, above and to the left of B — the omasum

rows.verbatim: A = Rumen
B = Abomasum
C = Omasum

notes: Figure opened and verified: agricultural-science-2021-OL-paper-p05-i0 carries the Question 2 heading, the sheep photograph, the full pink ruminant-stomach diagram with the A, B and C leaders, the printed word list (Omasum, Rumen, Abomasum) and the (a) instruction, ending at the 'C:' answer box. The letters are decoded to the scheme's own answers because the label-key panel renders only inside the post-reveal block. Q2 is 10 marks: 6 here (2 per letter, fixed) and 4 for part (b).

questionText: Identify the two types of soils shown in profile diagrams A and B above.
stem: Question 4 prints two cutaway soil profiles side by side under a pale banner heading the left column A and the right column B. The left profile is drawn to 3 m, the right to 2 m. Inside each profile the horizons are bracketed A, B and C and annotated: on the left 'Humus, rich dark brown colour', 'Stony' and 'Parent rock'; on the right 'Pale grey, heavily leached', 'Darker brown, leached minerals' and 'Parent rock'. Parts (b) and (c) then ask for one use of soil A and two disadvantages of soil B.

labelKey.meaning: the left-hand column — the soil the question calls A, a deep dark-brown profile over stony material: brown earth. (Inside each profile, A also brackets the top horizon: 'Humus, rich dark brown colour' on the left, 'Pale grey, heavily leached' on the right.)

the right-hand column — the soil the question calls B, a pale leached surface over an orange-brown band of redeposited minerals: podzol. (Inside each profile, B also brackets the middle horizon: 'Stony' on the left, 'Darker brown, leached minerals' on the right.)
the bottom bracket in both profiles, against the brick-patterned band — parent rock. C is not one of the soils the question asks you to name.

rows.verbatim: A = Brown earth
B = Podzol

notes: Figure opened and verified: agricultural-science-2021-OL-paper-p07-i1 carries the 'Question 4' heading, the lead line, the A/B banner, both annotated profiles with their depth scales, and the (a) instruction. The crop's letters are genuinely double-duty — A and B head the two COLUMNS (the soils being named) and also bracket the top and middle HORIZONS inside each profile — so the label key spells out both senses rather than leaving a student to guess which A the question means. Q4 is 10 marks: 4 here, 2 at (b), 4 at (c).

questionText: Where would you rank the greenhouse gas emissions from agriculture in 2018?
stem: Question 9 prints a doughnut chart of Ireland's greenhouse gas emissions in 2018, adapted from the Environmental Protection Agency (2020), and instructs: 'Analyse the chart and answer the question which follow.' Every sector on the chart carries its own percentage label, so the ranking is read off, not recalled. Parts (b) and (c) then ask for two sources of greenhouse gases from agriculture and for two ways of increasing biodiversity on a farm.

rows.verbatim: 1st (highest ranking) or most or top
rows.contextNote: The 'or's are three wordings of one answer, not three marks. A rank is wanted, not the percentage — but a student who writes '34%, the largest sector' has said the same thing and the examiner is directed to consider answers on their merits.

notes: Figure opened and verified: agricultural-science-2021-OL-paper-p12-i0 shows the Question 9 heading, the full stem, the complete doughnut chart with every sector labelled (Agriculture 34%, Transport 20%, Energy industries 17%, Residential 10%, Manufacturing Combustion 8%, Industrial processes 4%, F-gases 2%, Commercial Services 2%, Public Services 2%, Waste 1%), the EPA attribution and the (a) and (b) instructions. Bound because the answer is a chart reading — agriculture's 34% slice is the largest — and the figureless version of this part was deferred for exactly that reason. Filed under Evaluating evidence (1.3) rather than a farming topic, because the mark is for reading data.

questionText: Name the part labelled A on the diagram.
stem: Question 10 prints a side-view line drawing of the reproductive system of a cow and says: 'Look at the diagram and answer the questions which follow.' One structure is picked out by a short red arrow labelled A; the bladder and the vulva are already named on the drawing. Parts (b), (c) and (d) go on to ask for A's function, the cow's gestation and oestrous cycle lengths, and where the insemination gun must reach.

labelKey.meaning: the red arrow left of centre, pointing to the small oval body at the end of the coiled uterine horn — the ovary

rows.verbatim: Ovary
rows.contextNote: Printed in the scheme as 'Ovary*'. The SEC asterisk means only this exact term scores — 'egg sac' or a description does not — and a surplus wrong name written alongside it cancels this mark.

notes: Figure opened and verified: agricultural-science-2021-OL-paper-p13-i0 carries the Question 10 heading, the stem, the whole reproductive-tract drawing with the red A arrow and the 'Vulva' and 'Bladder' labels, and the (a), (b) and (c) instructions down to the 'Number of days' table head. Bound because 'the part labelled A' is unanswerable without seeing where the arrow points. Asterisked in the scheme, hence kind 'gate'.

questionText: Identify the structure located at B.
stem: Question 11 offers a choice of (a) or (b); this is part (a), introduced by 'The use of 3D plans are likely to become more common in the future development of new infrastructure of farms.' The figure is a three-dimensional aerial render of a dairy farmyard. Two structures are named on the render — the dairy cow collecting yard on the left and the cow cubicle house in the centre — and a red pointer coming in from the right-hand edge marks B. Parts (a)(ii) to (a)(iv) then ask for B's hazards, for a way the layout is economically sustainable, and for a labour-saving technology.

labelKey.meaning: the red pointer entering from the right-hand edge of the render, indicating the two long open-fronted bays on the right of the yard, filled to the brim and covered with dark plastic weighted down by tyres — a silage pit

rows.verbatim: Silage (pit)
rows.contextNote: 'Pit' is bracketed in the scheme, so 'silage' on its own scores; 'silage clamp' says the same thing.

notes: Figure opened and verified: agricultural-science-2021-OL-paper-p14-i0 carries the Question 11 choice line, the part (a) stem, the full 3D render with the 'Cow cubicle house' and 'Dairy cow collecting yard' callouts and the red B pointer, plus the (a)(i) and (a)(ii) instructions. The B pointer lands on two adjacent walled bays covered in dark sheeting held down by tyres — a silage pit, which is what the scheme awards. Bound because the question names a structure the student can only see.

questionText: Describe one environmental hazard and one potential safety hazard of structure B.
stem: Question 11 offers a choice of (a) or (b); this is part (a)(ii). The figure is a 3D aerial render of a dairy farmyard, with a red pointer from the right-hand edge marking B — the two walled bays covered in dark plastic and weighted with tyres that part (a)(i) identifies as the silage pit. The paper prints two answer lines, one headed 'Environmental:' and one headed 'Safety hazard:'.

labelKey.meaning: the red pointer entering from the right of the render, indicating the two walled bays covered with dark plastic and tyres on the right of the yard — the silage pit

rows.verbatim: Environmental hazard = (silage effluent) run off (into water sources)
rows.contextNote: The scheme prints '3+1' across the two hazards: the first correct hazard the examiner meets scores 3 and the second scores 1, so neither line can be given a fixed value. The solidus offers 'plastic wrapping' as an alternative environmental hazard, not as an extra mark.

rows.verbatim: Safety hazard = fall off silage pit or walls (no safety rails)
rows.contextNote: One safety hazard is wanted. 'machinery injury' is the scheme's alternative wording, not a second mark.

notes: Figure opened and verified: agricultural-science-2021-OL-paper-p14-i0. Bound because both hazards are hazards OF structure B, which is identifiable only from the render. Tariff is the scheme's '3+1', so orderedSplit with both rows null. Filed under Working safely (1.5) because the question is framed as hazards and the deck's other 2021 OL hazard cards sit there; a student revising silage storage (3.3.3) would also want it, since silage effluent run-off is a storage problem.

questionText: Which county has the highest % fluke damage?
stem: Question 13 opens with an article on liver fluke, then part (b) prints a map of the island of Ireland showing the incidence of liver fluke damage to beef cattle livers in the third quarter of 2020, from Beef HealthCheck slaughter data (adapted from Animalhealthireland, 2020). Counties are shaded by band, and three carry a percentage callout on the map. Part (b)(ii) then asks why the fluke damage in Cork is less than in more northern counties. Read the answer off the map — the shading and the callouts are the evidence.

rows.verbatim: Louth (at 17%)
rows.contextNote: Printed in the scheme as 'Louth* (at 17%)'. The SEC asterisk means only this county scores; the percentage in brackets contextualises it rather than being required. A surplus wrong county named alongside Louth cancels the mark.

notes: Figure opened and verified: agricultural-science-2021-OL-paper-p20-i0 carries the part (b) stem, the Beef HealthCheck map with its three callouts — Mayo 7.87%, Louth 17.0%, Cork 1.54% — the Animalhealthireland attribution, and the (b)(i) and (b)(ii) instructions. Bound because the answer is unreachable without reading the map; the deferred, figureless version of this part would have been a dangling reference. The companion part (b)(ii) already ships as a figureless card, since the question itself states the Cork/north comparison.

questionText: Complete the graph below by plotting the percentage germination of the grass seeds at 20 °C as calculated at part (a) and at 30 °C.
stem: Question 17(a) had a student investigate the effect of temperature on the percentage germination of certified grass seeds. One hundred seeds were sown at each of five temperatures (15, 20, 25, 30 and 35 °C) and the whole investigation was repeated four times. Part (a)(v) gave the number of seeds that germinated at 20 °C in the four trials — 62, 59, 61 and 58 — and asked for the mean percentage germination; that value is the one this part asks you to plot. The results table printed with the graph reads: 15 °C, 15 %; 20 °C, 'Calculated at part (a)'; 25 °C, 80 %; 30 °C, 65 %; 35 °C, 35 %. The bars for 15, 25 and 35 °C are already drawn; the 20 °C and 30 °C positions are blank.

rows.verbatim: Correct bar drawn at 20oC up to 60
rows.contextNote: The scheme awards 2 of these 3 marks where the value calculated at part (a)(v) was wrong but that wrong value is then plotted correctly — the plotting mark survives a bad calculation.

rows.verbatim: Correct bar drawn at 30oC up to 65
rows.contextNote: Read straight off the results table printed under the graph; no calculation is involved in this one.

notes: Figure opened and verified: agricultural-science-2021-OL-paper-p32-i0 shows the (b)(i) instruction, the complete bar chart 'Effect of Temperature on the Germination % of Grass Seeds' with a 0–85 axis in steps of 5, the three bars already drawn (15 at 15 °C, 80 at 25 °C, 35 at 35 °C) and the gaps at 20 and 30 °C, plus the results table with 'Calculated at part (a)' highlighted in the 20 °C cell. Bound because the answer is a plotting act on this printed chart. The stem deliberately carries the four raw trial counts rather than the mean, so the student still has to do part (a)(v)'s arithmetic to earn row 1. Filed under Communicating (1.4) — the mark is for presenting data, not for interpreting it.

questionText: The farmer aims to sell the lambs at a minimum average liveweight of 45 kg. Using the graph, determine the minimum number of weeks for the lambs to reach this liveweight.
stem: Question 18 — answer both (a) and (b), with either (c) or (d). Part (c): a farmer is producing early lambs for the Easter market. The lambs were born in January with an average birthweight of 4 kg and were weighed every two weeks. Part (c)(i) asked for their average daily liveweight gain over the 16-week period (112 days). The graph plots average liveweight in kilograms against age in weeks, from birth to week 16, with the y-axis marked every 5 kg. The question says 'using the graph', so the answer is a reading, and the paper prints a single 'Minimum number of weeks:' box for it.

rows.verbatim: 14 ( can be indicated on the graph)
rows.contextNote: The bracketed note is the examiner's: a candidate who marks the point on the graph instead of writing the number still scores. 'Minimum' matters — the lambs pass 45 kg at week 14, so week 16 is not the answer even though the lambs are heavier by then.

notes: Figure opened and verified: agricultural-science-2021-OL-paper-p35-i0 shows the (c)(ii) instruction, the whole line graph 'Average Liveweight Gain of Lambs from Birth to Slaughter' with all nine plotted points (Birth to week 16) and a 0–55 kg axis in steps of 5, and the 'Minimum number of weeks:' answer box. Bound because the question instructs the candidate to read this graph. The stem deliberately does NOT transcribe the liveweight table the paper also prints — that would hand over the reading the mark is for.

questionText: Identify which treatment group had the greatest effect on plant growth.
stem: Question 18 — answer both (a) and (b), with either (c) or (d). Part (d): a student investigated whether the nutrients N, P and K affected the growth rate of grass and barley plants, recorded the shoot length of multiple plants, calculated the mean and graphed the results. The bar chart plots average shoot length in centimetres against four treatment groups — Nutrients-NPK, N only, P only and K only — with a dark blue bar for barley and a yellow bar for grass in each group, every bar carrying its own value. Part (d)(i) asked why a mean was used; part (d)(iii) asks how the shoot length could have been measured. The answer here is one treatment group, read off the chart.

labelKey.meaning: Nitrogen — decoded in the key printed under the chart. It names the second treatment group, 'N Only'.
Phosphorus — decoded in the key printed under the chart. It names the third treatment group, 'P Only'.
Potassium — decoded in the key printed under the chart. It names the fourth treatment group, 'K Only'.

rows.verbatim: All nutrients (NPK)
rows.contextNote: The group the chart labels 'Nutrients - NPK'. It is the tallest pair on the chart for BOTH species, which is what makes it the answer — naming a group that is tallest for only one species does not score.

notes: Figure opened and verified: agricultural-science-2021-OL-paper-p37-i0 shows the 'Or' line, the part (d) stem, the full bar chart 'Effect of nutrients on growth of grass and barley plants' with the Barley/Grass legend and every bar valued (NPK 25/15, N only 15/9, P only 19/11, K only 21/12), the printed key 'N = Nitrogen  P = Phosphorus  K = Potassium', and the (d)(i) instruction. Bound because the batch flagged that the chart's series-to-value mapping could not be reconstructed from the extracted text with certainty — it can be read directly off this crop. The N/P/K letters are decoded from the key printed on the crop itself, not inferred. Filed under Evaluating evidence (1.3): the mark is for reading the chart.

questionText: Identify any four of the following breeds of animals.
stem: Section A, Question 2, part (a). Six colour photographs of farm animals are printed in two rows of three: A, B and C captioned above the top row, D, E and F captioned below the bottom row. Under them the paper prints an answer box running A: to F:. Only four of the six have to be named. Part (b), on selecting a female replacement animal for breeding, is carded separately.

labelKey.meaning: Top row, left - a long-bodied white pig standing side-on in a pen, metal railings behind it
Top row, centre - a sheep standing side-on on grass in front of a dry-stone wall, dense brown fleece, pale face, dark lower legs
Top row, right - a dapple-grey horse standing side-on on rough hillside grass
Bottom row, left - a single reddish-brown hen standing on grass
Bottom row, centre - a group of tan-coloured cattle standing together in a field
Bottom row, right - a black-and-white cow grazing in a field

rows.verbatim: A — Landrace
rows.contextNote: Photograph A, the pig. Any four of the six letters score 1 mark each; a fifth, wrong answer cancels a correct one.

rows.verbatim: B — Blue Leicester
rows.contextNote: Photograph B, the sheep. The scheme prints 'Blue Leicester'; the breed is usually written Bluefaced Leicester.

rows.verbatim: C — Connemara (pony)
rows.contextNote: Photograph C, the grey horse. Brackets in an SEC scheme mark words that are not required, so 'Connemara' on its own takes the mark.

rows.verbatim: D — Rhode Island red
rows.contextNote: Photograph D, the hen. The scheme prints 'red' in lower case; the breed name is normally capitalised as Rhode Island Red.

rows.verbatim: E — Limousine
rows.contextNote: Photograph E, the tan beef cattle. The scheme's spelling is 'Limousine'; the breed is normally written Limousin. Both name the same animal.

rows.verbatim: F — (Holstein) Friesian
rows.contextNote: Photograph F, the black-and-white dairy cow. 'Holstein' is bracketed, so 'Friesian' alone takes the mark.

notes: Figure opened before writing: agricultural-science-2022-HL-paper-p05-i0.png is the Question 2 breed grid, six photographs with A, B, C printed above the top row and D, E, F below the bottom row, exactly as the batch's candidate list describes. bestNofParts is used because the card shows all six lettered options while a student can only claim four - that is what the model exists for. 4 x 1 = 4 reconciles the tariff, and Q2 totals 10 with part (b)'s 2(3) = 6. The label key decodes which photograph each letter sits on rather than naming the breed, so the card does not give away its own answer before the student self-marks. Scheme lines: 'A = Landrace / B = Blue Leicester / C = Connemara (pony) / D = Rhode Island red / E = Limousine / F = (Holstein) Friesian', 4(1). Every row's text after the em dash was checked against the normalised scheme and found verbatim. MOVED FROM STEM (scheme side only): The scheme's front matter uses this exact question type as its worked example of the surplus-answer rule: a candidate who names five and gets one of them wrong scores 4 - 1 = 3, so there is nothing to gain from filling in all six.

questionText: A farmer identified different plants in the sward while measuring the grass. Identify any two of the following plants A, B or C from the sward.
stem: Section B, Question 13, part (a)(iii). Part (a) opens: 'Maintaining a constant supply of high quality leafy grass can be easily achieved by managing and measuring the amount of grass on the farm.' Parts (i) and (ii) covered the advantages of grass measuring and the kg DM/ha calculation; (iii) turns to what is actually growing in the sward. Three photographs are printed side by side in a bordered three-column table, with answer cells beneath reading A:, B: and C:. Only two of the three have to be named.

labelKey.meaning: Left cell - a close-up of one upright, densely packed green seed head, broad flat leaf blades behind it
Centre cell - several pale blue, daisy-like flowers on leafy stems, a bee on one of them
Right cell - a branched, open seed head of greenish-purple clustered spikelets on fine stems

rows.verbatim: A — Italian ryegrass
rows.contextNote: Photograph A, the single upright spiked seed head. Any two of the three letters score 1 mark each.

rows.verbatim: B — Chicory
rows.contextNote: Photograph B, the pale blue flowers. Chicory is the odd one out here - a deep-rooting herb sown in multi-species swards, not a grass.

rows.verbatim: C — Cocksfoot
rows.contextNote: Photograph C, the branched, clumped seed head on fine stems.

notes: Figure opened before writing: agricultural-science-2022-HL-paper-p20-i0.png carries the (iii) instruction in full plus the three-cell table of photographs with the A:, B:, C: answer cells beneath, so the crop is the whole question. bestNofParts fits exactly - three lettered options displayed, two claimable, 2 x 1 = 2 marks. Q13 reconciles as (a) 8 + 6 + 2 + 6 = 22 and (b) 12 + 4 + 8 + 4 = 28, total 50. Scheme: 'A = Italian ryegrass / B = Chicory / C = Cocksfoot', 2(1). Each row's text after the em dash was checked against the normalised scheme and found verbatim. The label key describes which photograph carries each letter without naming the plant, so the answer is not leaked before self-marking.

questionText: Identify three aspects of the shed which make it a suitable environment for calves and provide a reason for each aspect identified.
stem: Section B, Question 14, which is answered as 'both (a) and (b) with either (c) or (d)'. Part (c) opens: 'Analyse the picture of calf housing below and answer the questions which follow.' The photograph is taken inside a calf shed looking down the length of a straw-bedded pen: black-and-white calves lying and standing on deep clean straw, a low solid wall along the front of the pen with a galvanised barrier above it, spaced vertical timber boarding running along the upper side wall under the eaves, translucent roof panels letting daylight in, and a steel-framed pitched roof well above the calves. Three numbered answer slots are printed (1., 2., 3.), and each has to carry an aspect together with its reason - the question asks for both.

rows.verbatim: Space sheeting or high roof ‐ good airflow (ventilation)
accepts: board or concrete walls ensuring pen is draft free
(clean) roof lights ‐ plenty of natural light
large area with adequate lying space
clean bedding or smooth surfaces for good hygiene or disease reduction
long feed barrier ‐ adequate feeding space
rows.contextNote: 3(3) = any three aspects at 3 marks each. This row is a slot, not a required answer: any one of the six aspect-and-reason pairs the scheme prints takes the 3 marks, and the aspect alone does not - the question asks for a reason too.

rows.verbatim: board or concrete walls ensuring pen is draft free
accepts: Space sheeting or high roof ‐ good airflow (ventilation)
(clean) roof lights ‐ plenty of natural light
large area with adequate lying space
clean bedding or smooth surfaces for good hygiene or disease reduction
long feed barrier ‐ adequate feeding space
rows.contextNote: A second, different aspect. Ventilation without draughts is the pairing the picture is built around: air moves in high through the spaced boarding, while the solid lower wall keeps it off the lying calves.

rows.verbatim: (clean) roof lights ‐ plenty of natural light
accepts: Space sheeting or high roof ‐ good airflow (ventilation)
board or concrete walls ensuring pen is draft free
large area with adequate lying space
clean bedding or smooth surfaces for good hygiene or disease reduction
long feed barrier ‐ adequate feeding space
rows.contextNote: A third, different aspect. 'Clean' is bracketed, so it is not required - naming the roof lights and giving natural light as the reason is enough.

notes: Figure opened before writing: agricultural-science-2022-HL-paper-p25-i1.png is the Question 14(c) calf-housing photograph with the (c) and (i) instructions above it and the numbered answer grid below. The crop carries no letters, so labelKey is empty and the build files it as a question card carrying a figure rather than a diagram card. Tariff: scheme prints 3(3) = 9, and Q14 reconciles as (a) 10 + 2 + 3 + 3 + 4 = 22, (b) 6 + 8 = 14, (c) 9 + 5 = 14, total 50. The scheme prints six pooled aspect-and-reason pairs separated by solidi, so this is three slot rows with the pool in accepts, not six rows. Each row verbatim was checked against the normalised scheme and found contiguous. 'clean bedding or smooth surfaces for good hygiene or disease reduction' is NOT contiguous - the typeset marks cell '3(3)' lands between 'clean' and 'bedding' - so it appears only in accepts, which the build does not provenance-check. MOVED FROM STEM (scheme side only): the scheme's options are printed as aspect-and-reason pairs.

questionText: Identify breed E and F.
stem: Question 2 part (b) — the alternative to part (a). Jessica is a young sheep farmer and she is looking to buy a ram to breed replacements with her Suffolk cross ewes; two rams are photographed, lettered E and F. Parts (ii) and (iii) go on to ask which ram she should buy and why she keeps crossbred rather than purebred ewes.

labelKey.meaning: The ram in the left-hand photograph: tall and leggy with a long, bare, white face, a slightly Roman nose, upright ears, no wool on the head, and a tight curly tan-white fleece.
The ram in the right-hand photograph: short-legged, deep and blocky through the body with heavy hindquarters, a wide flat white face with black nose and black eye markings, and short erect ears.

rows.verbatim: E = Border Leister
rows.contextNote: The scheme spells it 'Leister'; the breed is the Border Leicester and the correct spelling is the same answer.

rows.verbatim: F = Texel or Beltex

notes: Bound to the p05 crop, opened and checked: it carries Jessica's stem sentence, both ram photographs with bold E and F above them, and the (i) answer boxes. The scheme prints a single '3+1' between the two answers and does not say which identification takes the 3, so this is an orderedSplit with both rows null — the first correct breed named scores 3 and the second 1. Q2 = 10 = 4 here + 4 for (b)(ii) + 2 for (b)(iii).

questionText: Identify the safety symbols labelled A and B above.
stem: Question 6 of Section A. The safety symbols shown are present on a selective herbicide used to control all species of docks in an established grassland sward (the crop also carries the paper's photograph of a dock plant growing in grass). Part (a) asks you to explain the underlined term 'selective herbicide' and part (c) asks for two precautions when applying herbicides.

labelKey.meaning: The left-hand pictogram: a red-outlined diamond standing on its point containing a solid black human torso and head, with a white star-burst radiating out of the chest.
The right-hand pictogram: a red-outlined diamond standing on its point containing a single bold black exclamation mark.

rows.verbatim: A = Health hazard / carcinogenic
rows.contextNote: One 2-mark point with two accepted wordings — 'health hazard' and 'carcinogenic' are the same mark, not two.

rows.verbatim: B = Harmful / caution / danger / warning / irritant
rows.contextNote: Five accepted wordings of the same 2-mark point. Any one of them scores it.

notes: Bound to the p09-i0 crop, opened and checked: it shows both GHS pictograms with the bold A and B beneath them and runs down to the (b) answer boxes, so it is the crop that actually carries what this part asks about. (p09-i1 is the same stimulus framed higher and is deliberately not used, so the two near-duplicate crops are never both bound.) The question text says 'labelled A and B', which is exactly the case the build refuses without a decoded label key — hence the labelKey above. Two mark digits of 2 printed against two separate answers, so a fixed tariff summing to 4; Q6 = 10 = 2 (a) + 4 here + 4 (c).

questionText: Identify what A, B and C are representing in the picture illustrating photosynthesis.
stem: Question 7 part (b) — the alternative to part (a). Photosynthesis is the method by which green plants make their own food using chlorophyll. In the picture a black arrow runs from the sun onto the leaves and a black arrow labelled 'Water' runs into the roots; the three arrows you are asked about are printed 'Gas A', 'Gas B' and 'C'. Part (ii) then asks for two ways a leaf is adapted to carry out photosynthesis.

labelKey.meaning: Printed on the picture as 'Gas A' — a black arrow travelling from the left-hand air INTO a leaf. The figure itself tells you it is a gas and that it is going in.
Printed on the picture as 'Gas B' — a pale arrow travelling OUT of the plant to the right, at the top of the shoot.
Printed on the picture as 'C' — a second pale arrow leaving the plant lower down and to the right. Unlike A and B it is not labelled 'Gas', so it need not be one.

rows.verbatim: A = Carbon dioxide (CO2)
B = Oxygen (O2) or water vapour
C = Glucose (C6H12O6) or oxygen or water vapour
rows.contextNote: The scheme lets the two outgoing arrows be answered either way round: whichever of oxygen and water vapour you did not use for B is accepted here, and glucose is accepted too.

notes: Bound to the p10-i1 crop, opened and checked: it carries the whole of part (b) — the stem sentence, the A/B/C answer boxes and the photosynthesis illustration with 'Gas A', 'Gas B', 'C' and 'Water' printed on it. Tariff '4+1+1' is printed once against the block of three answers with no statement of which letter takes the 4, so orderedSplit with all rows null: the first correct identification scores 4 and each further one 1. Q7(b) = 10 = 6 here + 4 for (b)(ii).

questionText: Identify each piece of equipment A and B above.
stem: Question 8 of Section A. A student was asked to carry out an investigation to isolate and grow bacteria from clover root nodules, and the two photographs show equipment the student may use. The later parts ask for a prediction, why the clover roots are washed in disinfectant first, and which bacterium in the nodules fixes nitrogen.

labelKey.meaning: The left-hand photograph: a long thin twisted-wire instrument with a plain handle at one end and a small closed circle of wire at the tip.
The right-hand photograph: shallow round clear plastic dishes with straight sides and a loose overlapping lid, shown empty.

rows.verbatim: A = Inoculating loop
B = Petri dish or agar plate

notes: Bound to the p11-i0 crop, opened and checked: it carries the Q8 stem, both equipment photographs with bold A and B above them, and the (a) answer boxes. Two separate mark digits of 2 in the scheme, so a fixed tariff summing to 4; Q8 = 10 = 4 here + 1 + 2 + 3 for (b), (c) and (d), all three already carded.

questionText: Identify each of the plants A and B.
stem: Question 16 part (c) of Section B — chosen instead of part (d). The pictures are of common plants found growing on Irish farms. Part (ii) then asks for one impact plant A has on farming or the environment, so the identification here decides what you can write there.

labelKey.meaning: The left-hand photograph: a single dense, rounded, dome-shaped head made up of dozens of small bright yellow daisy-like flowers, standing against dark green foliage.
The right-hand photograph: one upright leafless stalk rising out of grass, topped by a short dark brown-black cylindrical flower head ringed with a collar of tiny cream-white stamens.

rows.verbatim: A = Ragwort
B = Plantain or Ribwort

notes: Bound to the p31-i0 crop, opened and checked: it carries the (c) stem line, both plant photographs with bold A and B beneath them, and the (i) answer boxes. (p31-i1 is the same plate in a slightly taller window and is deliberately not used so the near-duplicate crops are never both bound.) The scheme prints '4+2' once, against A, with no statement of which plant takes the 4, so orderedSplit with both rows null. Q16(c) = 8 = 6 here + 2 for (c)(ii).

questionText: State one impact plant A has on farming or the environment.
stem: Question 16 part (c)(ii), following the plant plate in (c)(i): plant A is the yellow-flowered plant on the left of the pair, plant B the one on the right. One impact only is asked for and it is worth 2 marks, so a second impact adds nothing — and a wrong one written alongside a right one can cancel it.

labelKey.meaning: The left-hand photograph: a dense rounded dome of many small bright yellow daisy-like flowers against dark green foliage. This is the plant this part asks about.
The right-hand photograph: an upright leafless stalk topped by a short dark cylindrical head ringed with cream-white stamens. Printed on the same plate but not asked about here.

rows.verbatim: Noxious plant (harmful to animals)
rows.contextNote: One 2-mark point with three accepted wordings. Note the scheme accepts a POSITIVE impact as well as a negative one — supporting wildlife scores exactly the same as poisoning stock.

notes: Bound to the same p31-i0 plate as q16ci, because the answer depends entirely on which plant A is. The scheme prints one 2-mark line whose solidus separates three alternatives for the same point, so a single row with the other two in accepts rather than three rows inventing three marks. The third alternative is quoted in full in accepts even though the typeset mark digit splits it across two scheme lines ('supports many 2' / 'species of wildlife (biodiversity)') — accepts are not traced by the build, and the row's own verbatim is a contiguous span.

questionText: Identify each of the following plants commonly found on Irish farms.
stem: Question 16 part (d) of Section B — the alternative to part (c). Two photographs of plants commonly found on Irish farms are printed side by side, with the answer boxes lettered C (left) and D (right). Part (ii) then asks for one use for plant D.

labelKey.meaning: The left-hand photograph: a coarse plant in rough grass carrying several globular heads covered in spiny grey-green bracts, one open into a magenta-purple tuft and one withered brown, with prickly leaves.
The right-hand photograph: a ripe golden cereal against a blue sky, its seeds hanging singly on fine drooping stalks in a loose open head rather than packed onto a spike.

rows.verbatim: C = Thistle
D = Oats (wild)
rows.contextNote: 'Wild' is bracketed, so 'oats' alone scores. The loose drooping head is what separates oats from wheat or barley, whose seeds sit tight on a spike.

notes: Bound to the p31-i2 crop, opened and checked: it carries the 'Or', the (d)(i) instruction, both photographs, the lettered C and D answer boxes and the (d)(ii) instruction. (p31-i3 is the same plate in a near-identical window and is deliberately not used.) '4+2' is printed once, against C, without saying which plant takes the 4, so orderedSplit with both rows null. Q16(d) = 8 = 6 here + 2 for (d)(ii).

questionText: State one use for plant D.
stem: Question 16 part (d)(ii), following the plant plate in (d)(i): plant C is the spiny purple-headed plant on the left, plant D the ripe golden cereal on the right. One use only is asked for and it is worth 2 marks.

labelKey.meaning: The left-hand photograph: spiny grey-green globular heads, one open into a magenta-purple tuft, with prickly leaves. Printed on the same plate but not asked about here.
The right-hand photograph: a ripe golden cereal with its seeds hanging singly on fine drooping stalks in a loose open head. This is the plant this part asks about.

rows.verbatim: Animal feed
rows.contextNote: One 2-mark point with two accepted wordings — feeding stock and feeding people are the same mark here, not two.

notes: Bound to the same p31-i2 plate as q16di: the use asked for is the use of the plant you identified as D. One scheme line, one solidus, one 2-mark point — so one row with the alternative in accepts. Filed under 3.3.3 because it is about what the harvested cereal is used for rather than how it is identified; a taxonomy reviewer could reasonably move it to 3.2 alongside q16di.

questionText: Calculate the total bovine nitrogen (figure B) for all animals on John's farm for 2020-21.
stem: Question 17 part (b)(ii), from the same table as (b)(i). The right-hand column, 'Bovine nitrogen produced on John's farm', reads: suckler cows 2990 kg; cattle 0-1 year 1056 kg; cattle 1-2 year A, which you worked out in part (i) as 2280 kg; bull 1-2 year 57 kg; bull over 2 years 65 kg. Figure B is the bottom line of that column, 'Total bovine nitrogen produced on John's farm'. Show your calculation in the box.

rows.contextNote: All five livestock rows, including the 2280 you calculated in part (i). Leaving out the two single bulls is the common way to lose this.
The scheme adds: '(If a candidate gives 6448 (kg) without showing any calculations they may be awarded 6m)'.

notes: NO FIGURE, DELIBERATELY — same reasoning as q17bi: the stimulus is a typeset data table with no crop among this card's candidates, so the five addends are carried in the stem and figureKey is ''. Two mark digits of 3, so a fixed tariff summing to 6. Q17 = 50 = 18 for (a) + 8 + 6 + 6 + 6 for (b)(i)-(iv) + 6 for (c).

questionText: Identify which variety of perennial ryegrass produces the highest yield.
stem: Question 18 part (a) of Section B. The Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine (DAFM) produce a recommended list of perennial ryegrass seed varieties annually, and the paper prints two of them for you to analyse. Part (a)(i) asks for three of the physical traits the table assesses; this part sends you to one specific column of it.

rows.verbatim: Moyola (105 ton DM/ha)
rows.contextNote: Read the Total Yield column: Moyola 105, Genesis 103. Do not be pulled to Genesis by its bigger Spring Growth figure (118 against 109) — that is a different column. The scheme writes the unit as 'ton DM/ha'; the table heading is t DM/ha.

notes: Bound to the p35-i0 crop, opened and checked: it carries the Q18(a) stem, the DAFM logo and the full six-column variety table with both varieties' figures — Moyola 11 May, 105, 6.4, 109, 107, 100 and Genesis 12 May, 103, 6.7, 118, 102, 99.7. No letters on the crop, so labelKey is empty and this rides as a plain question card carrying a figure. One mark digit of 5 in the scheme, and 5 is what the paper allots. Filed under 1.3 (Evaluating evidence) rather than 3.3.1 because the whole task is reading a data table, matching agsci-2025-hl-q17cii; the sibling q18ai, which lists the traits from memory, stays at 3.3.1.

questionText: Identify which variety would produce more grass in autumn.
stem: Question 18 part (a)(iii), from the same DAFM recommended-list table as (a)(i) and (a)(ii). The table has six columns of data — Heading Date, Total Yield, Ground Cover, Spring Growth, Autumn Growth and % Dry Matter Digestibility — and this part names the season, which names the column.

rows.verbatim: Moyola (107 ton DM/ha)
rows.contextNote: Read the Autumn Growth column: Moyola 107, Genesis 102. The 105 in the scheme's answer to (a)(ii) came from Total Yield — quoting that figure here shows you read the wrong column, even though the variety happens to be the same one.

notes: Bound to the same p35-i0 crop as q18aii, since it is the same table. One mark digit of 5 in the scheme; Q18 = 50 = 12 + 5 + 5 for (a), 6 + 2 for (b) and 12 + 4 + 4 for (c). The trap this card exists to teach is column confusion: both answers are 'Moyola', but only one of the two figures is right for each part, and the scheme prints the figure alongside the variety.

questionText: Identify each of the following breeds of animals.
stem: Answer either (a) or (b). This is option (a): three colour photographs of cattle side by side, lettered A, B and C beneath, over an 'A: / B: / C:' answer table. The rest of option (a) then works off breed C — '(ii) Breed C is a dual-purpose breed' — and asks about buying a purebred bull.

labelKey.meaning: Left photograph — the heavily muscled bull with a roan red-and-white coat, broad white patches over the shoulder and flank, a dark red head and short horns, in front of a stone wall (Shorthorn)
Centre photograph — the heavily muscled black cow with irregular white patches over the back and flank and a white band across the face (Belgian Blue)
Right photograph — the tan/golden bull with a white face, white legs and a white tail switch (Simmental)

rows.verbatim: A — Short horn
rows.contextNote: This scheme's own worked example is a breed-identification question: a surplus WRONG breed written beside a correct one cancels the correct answer, so writing two names in one box costs the mark rather than hedging it.

rows.verbatim: B — Belgian Blue
C — Simmental

notes: Tariff 3(2) = three breeds at 2 marks each = 6, and Q1(a) reconciles as (i) 6 + (ii) 2 + (iii) 2 = 10. Crop opened and checked letter by letter before binding: A is the roan, short-horned bull, B the double-muscled black-and-white cow, C the tan-and-white bull — the same left-to-right order the scheme answers in. All three letters are asked about, so the 'also on the diagram' panel stays empty.

questionText: Identify each of the following breeds of animals.
stem: Answer either (a) or (b). This is option (b): three colour photographs lettered D, E and F beneath, over a 'D: / E: / F:' answer table. One is a dairy cow and two are sheep. Option (b) then moves on to the 'Fleckvieh Cattle' article and asks which Irish cattle industry that breed suits.

labelKey.meaning: Left photograph — the small fawn/light-brown cow with a dark muzzle ringed by a pale cream band, a dark tail switch and a visible udder, standing on grass beside a road (Jersey)
Centre photograph — the three sheep with dense white fleece and completely black faces, ears and legs (Suffolk)
Right photograph — the blocky, heavily muscled sheep with a bare white face, short white ears and white legs (Texel)

rows.verbatim: D — Jersey
rows.contextNote: This scheme's own worked example is a breed-identification question: a surplus WRONG breed written beside a correct one cancels the correct answer, so writing two names in one box costs the mark rather than hedging it.

rows.verbatim: E — Suffolk
F — Texel

notes: Tariff 3(2) = three breeds at 2 marks each = 6; Q1(b) reconciles as (i) 6 + (ii) 2 + 2 = 10. Crop opened before binding: D is the fawn dairy cow, E the black-faced sheep, F the white-faced meat sheep — the same left-to-right order the scheme answers in. Two of the three are sheep, which is what makes the question harder than it looks: it is titled 'breeds of animals', not 'breeds of cattle'.

questionText: Identify any two of the weeds that can be found in Irish fields using the list below.
stem: Question 2 opens with a five-panel diagram of the growth cycle of barley, which part (a) uses. Part (b) prints a word bank of three names — Chickweed, Charlock, Shepard's Purse (the paper's own spelling) — above three close-up photographs of flowering weeds, with an empty answer cell under each photograph. The photographs are not lettered: you write a name under each one, and only two of the three are needed.

rows.verbatim: Left photograph — Shepherd’s purse
rows.contextNote: The tall stalk carrying small four-petalled white flowers with flat, heart-shaped seed pods spreading below them. The paper's word bank spells it 'Shepard's Purse'; the scheme spells it 'Shepherd's purse'.

rows.verbatim: Centre photograph — Chickweed
rows.contextNote: The low, sprawling plant with broad oval pointed leaves and small white star-shaped flowers whose petals are deeply split.

rows.verbatim: Right photograph — Charlock
rows.contextNote: The bright yellow four-petalled flowers on a branched stem with coarse, toothed green leaves.

notes: Tariff 2(2) = any two at 2 marks each = 4, and Q2 reconciles as (a) 2(3) = 6 plus this 4. bestNofParts rather than fixed because all three photographs are shown and only two can be claimed. The scheme prints the answer as one row — 'Shepherd’s purse Chickweed Charlock' — in the same left-to-right order as the three answer cells under the photographs, which is how each row is anchored; the crop was opened and each plant checked against that order (pods = shepherd's purse, oval leaves and split white petals = chickweed, yellow crucifer = charlock).

questionText: Label the diagram below of the monogastric digestive system.
stem: Answer either (a) or (b). This is option (a): a cartoon side view of a pig, facing left, with its digestive tract drawn inside the body outline and three thick pale-blue arrows lettered A, B and C pointing into it, over an 'A: / B: / C:' answer table. Part (ii) then asks about the role of microorganisms in the same system.

labelKey.meaning: Arrow from the upper left into the large solid dark red organ sitting behind the chest (liver)
Arrow from above into the pale cream sac immediately behind and to the right of the red organ, where the oesophagus ends (stomach)
