Arrow from the lower right into the long narrow coiled tube filling the hindquarters (small intestine)

rows.verbatim: A — Liver
B — Stomach
C — Small intestine

notes: Tariff 3(2) = three labels at 2 marks each = 6, and Q10(a) reconciles as (i) 6 + (ii) 4 = 10. Crop opened before binding and each arrow traced to the organ it lands on: A on the solid red organ, B on the pale sac at the end of the oesophagus, C on the coiled tube. A labelling question is exactly the card type that must never ship without its diagram.

questionText: Identify the soil water content level for each diagram using the words in the box below.
stem: Answer both (a) and (b) with either (c) or (d). Part (b) prints three square schematics of a soil sample side by side under a blue banner carrying the letters A, B and C, with a word bank above them — Permanent wilting point, Field capacity, Saturation — and an empty answer cell under each schematic. The paper states the colour code: brown represents soil particles, blue represents water and white represents air spaces. Part (ii) then asks for the implications for a farmer of any two of the three states.

labelKey.meaning: Left schematic — blue water fills every gap between the brown particles and almost no white air space is left (saturation)
Centre schematic — only a thin blue film clings around each particle and most of the pore space is white air (permanent wilting point)
Right schematic — blue water holds in the narrow pores and around the particles while the wider pores are white air (field capacity)

rows.verbatim: A — Saturation
rows.contextNote: Order the three by how much blue is left, not by where they sit on the page: most water and no air = saturation, least water = permanent wilting point, and the middle one is field capacity.

rows.verbatim: B — Permanent wilting point
C — Field Capacity

notes: Tariff 3(3) = three at 3 marks each = 9. Q13 reconciles as (a)(i) 14 + (a)(ii) 12 + (b)(i) 9 + (b)(ii) 3 + (c) or (d) 12 = 50. The word bank prints the three terms in a DIFFERENT order from the answer (permanent wilting point, field capacity, saturation), so the card is useless without the crop — it was opened and each panel checked against the water/air ratio it draws before binding.

questionText: State the soil pH that produces the least amount of N20 emissions.
stem: A secondary school installed a new garden and polytunnel and the agricultural science class investigated the donated topsoil. Part (c) says 'Analyse the graph showing the effect soil pH has on nitrous oxide (N20) emissions and answer the questions which follow' and prints a bar chart titled 'Effect of soil pH on nitrous oxide (N20) emissions': cumulative N20 emissions in g N20/ha/year up the vertical axis, scaled 0 to 7000 in thousands, against four soil pH values along the bottom — 5.1, 5.4, 6.2 and 6.9. (The paper prints nitrous oxide as 'N20'.)

rows.contextNote: Asterisked in the scheme — printed as '*6.9'. Only that value scores, and a second value written beside it cancels this row. It is the shortest bar: emissions fall steadily as pH rises, from about 6500 g/ha/year at pH 5.1 to about 4000 at pH 6.9. The question asks for the pH, not the emissions figure.

notes: 6 marks on one asterisked value. Q15 reconciles as (a) 12 + (b) 6 + 3 + 7 + (c)(i) 6 + (c)(ii) 8 = 42 with (d) 8 = 50. Figure bound because the four pH values exist only on the chart's horizontal axis; the crop was opened and the bar heights read before writing the note.

questionText: Identify the main source of carbon emissions on the farm.
stem: Answer both (a) and (b) with either (c) or (d). As part of the governments' climate action plan targets, agriculture has to reduce its greenhouse gas emissions by 25% by 2030. Anna and Lucy examined the percentage share of the carbon emissions from their beef enterprise, which they received through their Bord Bia farmer feedback report, and the graph highlights where the emissions are coming from on their farm. It is a grouped bar chart, 'Percentage Share of Farm Carbon Emissions': percentage share (%) up the vertical axis, scaled 0 to 50, against four sources — Animal digestion, Manure usage, Fertiliser used, Forage / Feed — with three bars in each group: current farm assessment (2021), previous farm assessment (2019) and national average. (Adapted from Teagasc, 2022)

rows.verbatim: Animal digestion
rows.contextNote: Asterisked in the scheme — printed as '*Animal digestion'; only that term scores. It is the tallest group on the chart, at roughly 38% of the farm's emissions in both the 2021 and the 2019 assessment, against about 20% for manure and 16-17% for the other two.

notes: 5 marks on one asterisked term. Q16 reconciles as (a) 5 + 6 + 6, (b) 12 + 6, and (c) or (d) 15 = 50. Figure bound because nothing in the paper's text names the sources or their sizes — the ranking exists only in the bars, which were read off the opened crop.

questionText: Comment on the overall carbon emissions on the farm since Anna and Lucy joined the scheme and justify your answer.
stem: Question 16, part (a), third question on the same grouped bar chart: 'Percentage Share of Farm Carbon Emissions', with three bars for each of Animal digestion, Manure usage, Fertiliser used and Forage / Feed — current farm assessment (2021), previous farm assessment (2019) and national average. The two farm bars are what 'since Anna and Lucy joined the scheme' means: 2019 was the previous assessment, 2021 the current one.

rows.verbatim: Comment — Since Anna and Lucy joined the scheme, their carbon emissions have remained fairly constant
rows.contextNote: The 2021 bar sits level with the 2019 bar in all four groups, so the honest comment is 'no real change' — not 'improved'. A comment with no justification earns half the marks here.

rows.verbatim: Justify — No increase in emissions from any source
accepts: farm remains below national average in animal digestion and manure usage
farm emissions is still slightly higher than national average in fertiliser usage and forage or feed
correct use of percentages from graph
rows.contextNote: Any ONE of these justifications earns the 3 marks, and the scheme credits quoting the percentages off the graph as a justification in its own right.

notes: Tariff 2(3) = two parts at 3 marks each = 6: the comment, then one justification. The scheme lays the answer out under its own 'Comment' and 'Justify' headings, which is why the rows carry those labels. Figure bound because the whole answer is a bar-by-bar comparison of the 2019 and 2021 series against the national average.

questionText: Identify any two of the plant species commonly found in Irish multi species seed mixtures.
stem: Mark is reseeding 20% of his 150 hectare dairy and beef farm and researching which sward composition suits his soil type and enterprise. Part (b) is about the seed mixture; (b)(iii) prints three colour close-up photographs of plants side by side, each headed with a bold capital letter — A, B and C — over an empty three-cell answer row. Only two of the three are needed.

labelKey.meaning: Left photograph — a slender arching grass flowering head, straw-green fading to buff, with flattened spikelets set alternately edge-on along the stem (perennial ryegrass)
Centre photograph — leafless stalks each topped by a short dark cylindrical seed head ringed with a collar of white anthers (ribwort plantain)
Right photograph — bright blue, many-rayed daisy-like flowers on wiry branched stems (chicory)

rows.verbatim: A = Perennial ryegrass or PRG
B = (Ribwort) plantain
C = Chicory

notes: Tariff 2(2) = any two at 2 marks each = 4, so bestNofParts: three photographs shown, two claimable. Q17 reconciles as (a) 16 + 8, (b) 12 + 4 + 4, (c) 6 = 50. The scheme uses '=' between the letter and the name, so the rows keep that form. Crop opened before binding and each photograph checked: the seed head with alternate flattened spikelets is ryegrass, the dark heads ringed with white anthers are ribwort plantain, the blue rayed flowers are chicory.

questionText: Identify any two pieces of equipment labelled A, B or C required for this investigation.
stem: Question 1, part (a). An agricultural science student wanted to test the pH of a sample of soil before deciding what crops to sow. The paper draws the whole bench of apparatus. Two items are already named in words on the drawing — the pH probe (its display reading 6.5) and the Universal Indicator — and three more are picked out by blue arrows lettered A, B and C. Only the lettered three are claimable, and the paper prints an answer line for each of A, B and C even though any two score.

labelKey.meaning: pH paper or (universal) indicator paper — the yellow/orange test strip standing upright in a small beaker of pale filtrate, its submerged tip turned green
Graduated cylinder — the tall measuring cylinder with a filter funnel of dark soil sitting in its mouth
Electronic or mass balance — the flat balance with a soil sample on the pan, its display reading 100.00 g

rows.verbatim: A — pH paper or (universal) indicator paper
rows.contextNote: The scheme's "or" here offers two names for one item, not two marking points — pH paper and universal indicator paper are the same strip. A arrows the yellow strip in the beaker of soil filtrate whose submerged tip has gone green.

rows.verbatim: B — Graduated cylinder
rows.contextNote: B arrows the tall graduated tube with the filter funnel of soil resting in its mouth — it is catching the filtrate. This point is not asterisked, so the SEC's general synonym rule applies to how the apparatus is named.

rows.verbatim: C — Electronic or mass balance
rows.contextNote: Again one item with two names, not two points. C arrows the balance under the soil sample, reading 100.00 g — it is how the fixed mass of soil is weighed out before water is added.

notes: Bound to agricultural-science-2023-OL-paper-p03-i0, which I opened before writing: it is the Question 1 bench drawing and it carries this part's own A:/B:/C: answer table underneath, so it is unambiguously this question's figure. Verified on the image: blue arrow A → the upright yellow/orange test strip in a beaker of pale liquid with a green submerged tip; arrow B → the tall graduated cylinder with a filter funnel of dark soil in its mouth; arrow C → the electronic balance with a soil sample on the pan reading 100.00 g. The 'pH probe' (display 6.5) and 'Universal Indicator' (pipette in a beaker) are labelled in words, NOT lettered, so they are not claimable answers here. Tariff: the scheme prints '2(3)' against the block of three lettered answers — three options are displayed but only two can be claimed, at 3 marks each = 6, which is exactly what bestNofParts exists for. Each of the scheme's three lines uses a plain 'or' between two names of the same instrument; none of them is a solidus list of separate points.

questionText: Identify which sustainable reseeding method has the highest potential for grass production.
stem: Question 13, part (b)(i), Section B. The paper's lead-in reads: traditional reseeding methods involve mainly ploughing the land; research into more sustainable practices (disc, one pass and direct drill) is shown in the graph; the sustainable practices are being compared to ploughing, which has a grass growth potential of 1. The column chart is titled 'Comparison of reseeding methods in terms of grass production potential', with 'Grass production relative to plough method' up the y-axis from 0 to 1.2 and 'Reseeding method' along the x-axis. Its four bars carry printed data labels: Plough 1, Disc 1, One pass 0.95, Direct drill 0.87. Source: (Adapted from Teagasc, 2022).

rows.verbatim: Disc
rows.contextNote: Plough also reads 1 on the graph, but plough is the traditional method the others are being measured against — the question asks which SUSTAINABLE method is highest, and the paper names those as disc, one pass and direct drill. Of those three, disc reads 1, one pass 0.95 and direct drill 0.87, so disc matches ploughing outright. Answering "plough" reads the tallest bar rather than the question.

notes: Bound to agricultural-science-2023-OL-paper-p21-i0, opened before writing. Verified on the image: the (b) stem naming disc, one pass and direct drill as the sustainable practices and ploughing as the benchmark of 1; a four-bar column chart over a faded photograph of a grazing field, titled 'Comparison of reseeding methods in terms of grass production potential'; y-axis 'Grass production relative to plough method' gridded 0 to 1.2; legend Plough / Disc / One pass / Direct drill; printed data labels 1, 1, 0.95, 0.87 above the blue, green, pink and yellow bars in that order; caption '(Adapted from Teagasc, 2022)'; and beneath it the (i) and (ii) instruction lines, which ties the crop to this question. No letters appear on this crop, so labelKey is empty and the card rides as a plain question card carrying a figure. Tariff: the scheme prints a bare 6 against 'Disc'.

questionText: Briefly explain one reason why handling facility B is better for animal movement.
stem: Answer either (a) or (b). The picture shows different cattle handling facilities. Analyse the pictures and answer the questions that follow. Part (i) asked for one use of cattle handling facilities on the farm; part (iii) then asks about the head gate arrowed in picture A.

labelKey.meaning: photograph of a straight galvanised steel race and crush built along a yard wall, with an orange callout arrow labelled "Headgate" pointing at the gate at the end of the race
plan-view drawing of a curved single file race leading out of a round crowd pen, with the curve marked "Right way", a straight dashed path marked "Wrong way", and the note "Cattle see place to go"

rows.verbatim: (As the animals go around the curve) they think they are going back to where they came from
accepts: the animals cannot see people and other moving objects (at the end of the chute)
it takes advantage of the natural circling behaviour of cattle
one-way system for ease of movement
rows.contextNote: One reason only is asked for — any one of the scheme's four wordings scores the full 3 marks.

notes: Flat 3-mark tariff, so fixed with a single row. The scheme's four solidus-separated reasons are alternative wordings of ONE 3-mark point, not four points, so they sit in accepts rather than in four rows. The displayed verbatim is the first alternative because it is the only one whose text does not run across the scheme's inline mark digit. Figure p05-i0 opened and checked before binding: picture A is the straight race photograph with the orange 'Headgate' callout, picture B is the curved-race plan view with 'Right way' / 'Wrong way' paths — the comparison the question turns on. Letter A is decoded but marked not-asked, since this part asks only about B.

questionText: Label any three parts of the diagram using the words in the list below.
stem: The diagram shows the digestive system of a calf. Analyse the diagram and answer the questions that follow. The oesophagus is already named on the diagram and is not one of the four lettered parts; the word bank printed under the diagram is Omasum, Abomasum, Rumen, Reticulum. Part (b) then asks for the first feed required by the calf.

labelKey.meaning: the rounded orange sac in the middle of the abdomen, sitting between the yellow compartment in front of it and the brown one behind it
the large yellow sac filling the upper front of the abdomen, above where the blue oesophagus runs in
the large brown sac at the back of the abdomen, which also runs forward along the floor of the belly
the smaller gold lobe at the lower front of the yellow area, just behind and below the point where the oesophagus enters

rows.verbatim: A — Omasum
B — Rumen
C — Abomasum
D — Reticulum

notes: Tariff '3(2)' with a question that asks for ANY THREE of four lettered parts, so bestNofParts: four rows are displayed, three are claimable at 2 marks each = 6, which is what Q5 allots to part (a) (the other 4 marks are part (b)). Figure p07-i0 opened before writing: a cartoon calf in side view with four black leader arrows, and the letter-to-compartment mapping in the rows is the scheme's own (A Omasum, B Rumen, C Abomasum, D Reticulum) — the label key describes only where each arrow lands, so it does not pre-empt the answer. The abomasum being drawn as the largest compartment is correct for a CALF, which is what the paper says the diagram shows.

questionText: Identify any three of the following breeds using the list below.
stem: Answer either (a) or (b). The photographs below show some breeds of sheep found on Irish farms, with the word bank Texel, Suffolk, Charolais, Border Leicester printed above them. Only three of the four letters need to be named. Part (ii) then asks for one reason why a named breed is suitable for sheep meat production.

labelKey.meaning: top left — a stocky cream-coloured ram standing side-on in a grassy paddock with autumn trees behind, pale face and pale legs, wool right down over the body
top right — two white-faced sheep photographed head-on, with long upright ears and Roman (convex) noses, standing in a coastal field
bottom left — a short, heavily muscled ram held by a handler, with a bare white face and white legs and a very deep, blocky body
bottom right — a white-fleeced sheep with a black head and black legs standing side-on in a dry paddock

rows.verbatim: A — Charolais
B — Border Leicester
C — Texel
D — Suffolk

notes: Tariff '3(2)' against 'identify any three', so bestNofParts — four options displayed, three claimable at 2 each = 6, leaving 4 marks for part (a)(ii) out of the 10 for Q6. Figure p08-i1 opened before writing: the word bank plus the two-by-two photograph grid, all four letters legible and uncut. Letter-to-breed mapping is the scheme's. The scheme spells the breed 'Charolais' here and 'Charollais' in part (ii); this card reproduces the (i) spelling as printed. MOVED FROM STEM (scheme side only): under the scheme's surplus-answer rule a wrong extra answer cancels a correct one.

questionText: State with reason which cow A or B a farmer would choose to cross with the Belgian Blue bull shown in the picture above.
stem: Answer either (a) or (b). The picture at the head of part (b) — not carried in this crop — shows the Belgian Blue beef breed: an extremely heavily muscled, double-muscled continental bull, white to pale roan in colour. Part (i) asked for two of its physical characteristics.

labelKey.meaning: left — a fawn/tan cow grazing head-down, fine-boned and angular with a large well-filled udder and a pale tail switch
right — a large white-cream cow standing facing the camera, deep and thick through the shoulder and hindquarter with a broad frame

rows.verbatim: Cow: B or Charolais
rows.contextNote: The scheme accepts either the letter or the breed name.

rows.verbatim: Big frame
rows.contextNote: Reason — any ONE of the scheme's three reasons scores the 2 marks. All three say the same thing: she is big enough to calve down to a double-muscled bull.

notes: Tariff '2(2)' = the cow (2) plus the reason (2) = 4, fixed. Figure p15-i1 opened before binding and it carries the part (ii) instruction line and both lettered photographs; p15-i2 is a one-pixel-taller duplicate of the same crop and is left unbound so the two do not collide on hash. The bull photograph sits on the same page but in a separate crop (p15-i0), so what it shows is carried in the stem instead — the question's phrase 'shown in the picture above' would otherwise dangle. Reason row keeps the scheme's three solidus alternatives as accepts rather than as extra rows, which would inflate a 4-mark part to 8.

questionText: Briefly outline one reason for your choice in part (i).
stem: Silage making is a very important aspect of farm life as it is an essential feedstuff for ruminant animals on farms. Part (b)(i) printed the two grass photographs below and asked which shows the correct stage of cutting the grass for silage.

labelKey.meaning: left — a stemmy, pale sward that has run to seed, with many tall stems carrying open branched seed heads standing above the leaves
right — a dense, deep-green sward of broad leaf blades with no stems or seed heads showing

rows.verbatim: Leafy grass
rows.contextNote: One reason only — any ONE of the scheme's three scores the full 2 marks. A candidate who ticked A in part (i) scores by naming the opposite point (stemmy, seed heads out, less digestible).

notes: Flat 2-mark tariff, fixed, one row. The scheme's three solidus alternatives are one point stated three ways and live in accepts. Figure p22-i1 opened before binding: it carries the part (b)(i) instruction and both lettered close-ups, A headed out and B leafy — which is exactly what the reason turns on, so the card cannot stand without it. The same crop is bound by the (b)(iii) card, which is allowed because it is the same figure key. Part (b)(i) itself is skipped: its scheme entry is a bare tick with no answer text. MOVED FROM STEM (scheme side only): The marking points here are the ones credited for choosing photograph B; the scheme adds '(Allow opposite points for A)'.

questionText: Identify the growth stage of plant B by placing a tick (✓) in the correct box. [Inflorescence / Vegetative / Elongation]
stem: Silage making is a very important aspect of farm life as it is an essential feedstuff for ruminant animals on farms. Part (b)(i) printed the two grass photographs below; this part asks about photograph B only. The three options are printed as text boxes on the paper and are reproduced in the question.

labelKey.meaning: left — a stemmy, pale sward that has run to seed, with many tall stems carrying open branched seed heads standing above the leaves
right — a dense, deep-green sward of broad leaf blades with no stems or seed heads showing

rows.verbatim: Vegetative
rows.contextNote: The box the scheme ticks. Photograph B is all leaf with no stem elongation and no seed head showing, so the sward is still vegetative.

notes: Flat 2-mark tick-box. The three options are TEXT on the paper, so unlike (b)(i) this part has a real answer in the scheme ('Vegetative') and is fully cardable; the options are transcribed into questionText as printed. The figure is still needed because 'plant B' is a dangling reference without it — p22-i1 was opened and carries both lettered photographs. Letter A is decoded but marked not-asked, so the student still leaves with the whole figure read.

questionText: Label the diagram of the ewe reproductive system using the list of words in the box below.
stem: Answer both (a) and (b) with either (c) or (d). The breeding season is an important and busy time on sheep farms to ensure successful lamb production. Part (a)(i) asked about the management of the ewe at mating. All four lettered parts are to be labelled here, from the word bank Ovary, Uterus, Fallopian tube, Cervix.

labelKey.meaning: arrow into the thick pink horn-shaped structure at the top left of the tract, the body and horns seen from the front
arrow to the fine coiled tube at the outer end of the left horn, just before the small pale round body
arrow to the small pale round body at the outer end of the right horn
arrow to the narrow ridged neck on the midline, where the body of the tract narrows into the passage below it

rows.verbatim: A — Uterus
B — Fallopian tube
C — Ovary
D — Cervix

notes: Tariff '4(3)' = four labels at 3 marks each = 12, and the question asks for all four (not 'any three'), so this is fixed, not bestNofParts — the rows sum exactly to the tariff. Figure p25-i1 opened before binding: the front-view illustration with four blue leader arrows and the word bank beside it, all four letters legible. Letter-to-part mapping is the scheme's own; the label key describes only where each arrow lands. Note the scheme heads this part 'the female reproductive system' while the paper prints 'the ewe reproductive system' — the paper's wording is used for questionText.

questionText: Using the colours in the box below, list the colours in order of sequence used by the farmer during mating.
stem: Answer both (a) and (b) with either (c) or (d). At mating the farmer straps a raddle on the ram to mark the ewes that have been served, and part (b)(iii) established that the colour is changed every 13–15 days so that any ewe repeating shows up. The answer table on the paper has three rows: 1st colour, 2nd colour, 3rd colour.

labelKey.meaning: left — a 1 kg tub of pale green raddle powder
centre — a 1 kg tub of pale blue raddle powder
right — a 1 kg tub of pale yellow raddle powder

rows.verbatim: 1st colour — Yellow / C
rows.contextNote: The sequence runs lightest to darkest so that each new mark shows up over the one before it.

rows.verbatim: 2nd colour — Green / A
3rd colour — Blue / B

notes: The scheme prints the tariff as '4 + 1 + 1' for a 6-mark part without saying which colour carries which value — under the scheme's own front matter the FIRST correct answer encountered takes the 4 — so this is orderedSplit and every row is marks: null. Putting 4/1/1 on specific rows would be a claim the scheme does not make. Figure p26-i0 opened before binding: three identical 1 kg raddle tubs headed A (green), B (blue), C (yellow), which is what makes the scheme's 'Yellow / C' pairing readable. The solidus in each row separates two wordings of one answer (the colour or its letter), not two marking points. MOVED FROM STEM (scheme side only): The scheme accepts either the colour name or the letter of the tub.

questionText: Identify the breed of dairy cow shown in the picture below.
stem: Answer both (a) and (b) with either (c) or (d). Calving is a very busy time on all beef and dairy farms, so it is important for farmers to be prepared in advance. Parts (a)(i) and (a)(ii) dealt with preparing for the calving season and with the practices carried out on the calf at birth.

rows.verbatim: (Holstein) Friesian
rows.contextNote: The brackets are the scheme's: 'Friesian' alone is enough, and 'Holstein Friesian' is equally acceptable.

notes: Flat 6-mark tariff, one answer, fixed. Figure p34-i0 opened before binding: the part (iii) instruction line above a single photograph of a black-and-white cow grazing, lean and angular with a large udder — no letters on it, so the card carries a figure with an empty label key and stays a question card rather than a diagram card. Nothing in the photograph is cut.

questionText: Identify the hormone labelled X responsible for milk let down.
stem: Question 13, part (d) — answered instead of part (c). The paper prints: 'A hormone is responsible for milk let down in cows. Analyse the picture and answer the questions that follow.' The picture below is that picture. Part (ii), printed under the same picture, then asks for one trigger of milk let down.

rows.verbatim: Oxytocin

notes: Figure opened before writing (public/exam-figures/agricultural-science/markbank/agricultural-science-2025-HL-paper-p24-i0.png): a cut-out side view of a black-and-white Holstein Friesian facing right, with a red pathway overlaid — a solid red dot high on the head behind the poll, a heavy red dashed line running down the neck to a point at the shoulder, then back horizontally along the underline, then down to a red arrowhead at the udder. A blue-outlined label box reading 'Hormone X' sits lower right with a solid red arrow pointing at the shoulder bend of that pathway. Parts (i) and (ii) with their blank answer boxes are printed beneath the picture on the same crop, so the student sees the question exactly as the paper set it. Scheme p.18 prints a single answer, 'Oxytocin', against the full 5 marks — one row, fixed tariff, no solidus and no alternatives to split. labelKey decodes X so the build's lettered-parts guard is satisfied; askedInThisQuestion is true because X is precisely what this part asks for, which also keeps the 'Also on the diagram' panel from printing the answer. The companion card agsci-2025-hl-q13dii (part (ii), milk let-down triggers) already exists and carries no figure, so this crop is bound exactly once in the subject deck.

questionText: Identify A and B in the chart above of the composition of milk.
stem: Question 15, part (b). A north Clare dairy farm sells its value-added milk to local people through a milk vending machine, and to produce milk for human consumption it must be of the highest standard. The chart shows the typical composition of cow's milk. Its five sectors carry the values 3.40%, 4.00%, 87.5%, 4.20% and 0.90%; the legend names three of them — Protein, Lactose and Minerals — and leaves the other two lettered A and B. The paper's answer table has one column, Component, with a row for A and a row for B.

labelKey.meaning: The 4.00% sector, drawn in purple and pulled out from the pie — (butter) fat.
The large green 87.5% sector that forms the body of the pie — water.

rows.verbatim: A: (Butter) fat
rows.contextNote: The bracketed word is context, not a requirement — "fat" scores.

rows.verbatim: B: Water

notes: Figure opened and checked by eye: agricultural-science-2025-OL-paper-p25-i0.png is this part's own exploded pie, titled "Average Milk Composition", with the red bold B inside the 87.5% green sector and the white A on the 4.00% purple sector, the legend listing Protein, A, B, Lactose and Minerals, and the Component answer table underneath. The percentages extract as text but which value carries A and which carries B is only readable from the chart, so the crop is what makes the part answerable. Tariff: the scheme prints a single combined "4+2" against the A and B lines, so no per-row value is claimed — same treatment as sibling part (b)(ii), whose "5+2" was also modelled as an ordered split. Q15 reconciles as 13 (part a) + 12 + 7 + 6 (part b) + 12 (part c) = 50.

questionText: Identify one way in which the farm in the photograph could become more energy efficient.
stem: Question 4 opens "Study the photograph of the farm layout below and answer the questions which follow." Beneath that line the paper prints one oblique aerial colour photograph of a working Irish farmyard — house, sheds, yard, storage and the surrounding grass fields — and all three parts of Question 4 are answered from that single photograph. The crop stops after the printed text of this part, so parts (b) and (c) are not shown. Question 4 is worth 10 marks; this part carries 2.

rows.verbatim: Solar panels / increase amount of roof lights or sky lights or reduce the need for artificial light / install windmill / install bio‐digester
rows.contextNote: One 2-mark point; every alternative the scheme separates with a solidus is a different way of earning the same 2. The scheme's list is not closed — it ends with the examiner instruction "other valid answer" — so a sensible energy measure you can justify from this yard scores even though it is not printed. That permission is what openList records here.

notes: Figure opened and checked: agricultural-science-2021-HL-paper-p08-i0.png is the Question 4 aerial farmyard photograph together with its heading and the printed text of part (a). The question says "the farm in the photograph", so it is a dangling reference without the crop. One row: the scheme prints a single 2 for the whole list, and openList is set because the scheme itself ends with "other valid answer" — that phrase is an examiner instruction, not a wording a candidate could write, so it is encoded by openList alone and is no longer carried in accepts. The only remaining accepts entry is the scheme's own fifth alternative, "rainwater harvesting". The stem was also cut back to context — where the question sits, what kind of image it is, the tariff — because its earlier inventory of the yard called out the shed's rooflights, which is one of the scheme's own marking points.

questionText: State two ways in which the farmyard is suited to economy of labour.
stem: Question 4 continued, answered from the same aerial photograph of the farm layout printed at the head of the question. notes: Bound to the inspected Question 4 crop agricultural-science-2021-HL-paper-p08-i0.png. Every answer the scheme allows is an observation read off that photograph — sheds close together, bales and pit beside the sheds, cow housing close to the parlour — so the part is unmarkable without it. Modelled as fixed 2(2) with two displayed rows at 2 each and the remaining four of the scheme's six options in accepts on both rows. Both displayed verbatims are now excluded from the shared accepts pool, matching the file's existing fixed 2(2) precedent at 2021 HL Q2(a)(iii); previously each row's accepts held the other row's verbatim, which let a single scheme option be self-awarded on both rows for 4 marks where the scheme awards 2. bestNofParts is not used because only two rows are displayed and a student can claim both. The stem was also cut back to context: it previously described the house above the yard, the sheds adjoining each other, the bales beside the sheds and the roadways to the fields — four of the six marking points, handed over before the student answered.

questionText: What is meant by this farm safety sign?
stem: Question 8 offers a choice of (a) or (b); this is part (a)(ii). Part (a) opens: 'As part of the Bord Bia Quality Assurance Schemes, farmers must ensure that all of their medicines are locked away in a medicine cabinet', and (a)(i) asked why. The sign this part asks about is printed on its own in the right-hand margin beside the (a)(ii) answer box — a yellow triangular warning sign with a heavy black border and a single black pictogram inside it. The photograph of an open medicine cabinet higher up the crop belongs to part (a)(i), not to this part.

rows.verbatim: Danger overhead power lines
rows.contextNote: The solidi separate three wordings of ONE 2-mark point — the sign has one meaning, and any one of the three carries the whole 2. A second, wrong meaning written beside a right one cancels the mark.

notes: Figure opened and verified: agricultural-science-2021-OL-paper-p10-i0 shows the Question 8 choice line, the part (a) stem, the (a)(i) answer box with its medicine-cabinet photograph, the (a)(ii) instruction and the yellow triangular sign in the right margin, whole and untruncated. The stem says plainly which image belongs to which part so the student is not left guessing. Bound because the whole question is 'what does THIS sign mean'. The scheme's third wording, 'electric shock risk', is now in accepts; it cannot be the row verbatim because the scheme file typesets the marks cell inside it ('… / electric 2' then 'shock risk'), which I checked against the file — but accepts is not traceability-checked, so there was never a reason to withhold it. The stem describes the sign as a yellow triangle with a black pictogram rather than naming the pictogram, since naming it is most of the answer. Part (b)(i) asks about a DIFFERENT sign on page 11 with a different answer ('Caution farm machinery'); no p11 crop exists on disk (verified), so that part is skipped rather than bound to this one.

questionText: Identify the best quality silage and state for which animals this silage is suitable.
stem: Question 6, part (a)(ii). Question 6 offers (a) or (b); this is the (a) route, and part (i) has already asked about the letters BCS that run through the captions. The diagram shows the grass growth cycle and how each growth stage affects silage quality: five drawings of a grass plant run left to right from a short leafy tuft to a tall stem that has headed out, an orange bar beneath them carries the letters A, B, C and D, and under that the row labelled 'Silage % Dry Matter Digestibility (DMD)' brackets a band of DMD figures beneath each letter together with the class of animal that band suits. The paper prints two answer lines, 'Silage quality:' and 'Animal:'.

labelKey.meaning: the first bracket from the left in the 'Silage % Dry Matter Digestibility (DMD)' row, sitting at the young, leafy end of the growth cycle; the only one of the four brackets that spans two DMD columns, and it carries a single animal caption
the second bracket, one DMD column wide, with a single animal caption
the third bracket, one DMD column wide, carrying two animal captions
the fourth and rightmost bracket, at the mature, stemmy, headed-out end of the growth cycle; one DMD column wide, carrying two animal captions

rows.verbatim: Best quality silage = 76%+ DMD or A
rows.contextNote: The scheme's "or" gives two ways of naming one band — the DMD figure or the letter — so either alone takes the 2. Quality falls left to right as the grass matures, so the best silage comes from the leafiest, least mature grass; on the chart that bracket is the only one spanning two DMD columns, and its upper column is the top of the scale.

rows.verbatim: Suitable animals = freshly calved dairy cows in winter milk
rows.contextNote: This is the caption the paper prints under the band named in the first row, and it has to match that band — reading the animals off a neighbouring bracket loses this mark even if the band itself was named correctly.

notes: Bound to agricultural-science-2023-OL-paper-p08-i0, opened before writing; each letter's horizontal position was checked against its own bracket rather than assumed from the ordering — A sits over the red bracket spanning the 76+ and 74-76 columns, B over the blue bracket at 72, C over the red bracket at 69-70, D over the blue bracket at <67. Two defects fixed. First, the stem expanded BCS as 'body condition score', which is the first marking point of Q6(a)(i), a 6-mark card in the same deck, and the stem renders above the question before the student answers (SessionScreen.tsx:890); the stem now records only that part (i) has already asked about those letters. Second, D carries askedInThisQuestion:false here, so its entry rendered in the reveal's 'Also on the diagram' panel and read '<67' plus 'Suckler cows requiring no BCS gain' — the entire answer to the sibling Q6(a)(iii) card. Every entry is now structural: which bracket the letter sits over, how many DMD columns it spans and how many animal captions it carries, with no DMD figure and no caption text. C and D both carry two captions, so nothing in the panel discriminates between them either. Tariff: the scheme prints a 2 in the marks column against the silage line and a 1 against the animal line, each tied to its own content, so this is fixed, not an ordered split. Paper wording of the question confirmed against page 8 of the PDF ('state for which animals this silage is suitable').

top right — a clump of large, broad, oval leaves with wavy margins and a stout pale midrib, growing out of grass
bottom left — a low mat of rounded three-part leaves beaded with rain, with one round white flower head on a short stalk
bottom right — a close-up of a single flowering grass head, a slim spike with spikelets set alternately along it

notes: Tariff '3(4)' against 'identify any three', so bestNofParts — four plants shown, any three claimable at 4 marks each = 12, and Q13's parts sum to the printed 50 with this part at 12. Figures p20-i0 and p20-i1 are the same grid; both were opened, and p20-i1 is the one bound because p20-i0 runs on past the letters into the answer lines 'A:' and 'B:' below the photographs, which would put two undecodable letters on the crop. The scheme prints the four answers as 'Nettle', 'Dock leaf', 'Clover' and 'Perennial Ryegrass' and credits no alternative wordings. The paper's own word box prints two of them at greater length — 'Broad leaf dock' and 'White clover' — so that difference is recorded as a contextNote on those two rows and NOT as accepts: accepts renders inline as 'Dock leaf or Broad leaf dock', which would show the student a scheme alternative that the scheme does not contain.

questionText: Outline how any four benefits can improve agricultural productivity and/or ecosystem health.

Improved access to soil nutrients improves crop quality / increases protein or vitamin or mineral content of food crops / produces healthier feed for livestock or higher quality produce for consumers.

stem: Beef farmers Dylan and Margaret are aiming to improve the sustainability and profitability of their suckler-to-beef enterprise. questionText: Outline with reason one risk of grazing high-clover swards for beef cattle.

questionText: Outline two management practices to maintain clover in a grass–clover sward under grazing conditions.

rows.verbatim: Maintain correct soil pH (around 6.3–6.5) / ensure adequate P and K levels / controlled nitrogen use (as this favours grass growth and suppresses clover) / rotational grazing – (use a tight grazing system) to prevent shading / avoid overgrazing in wet conditions or prevent poaching which damages clover / reseeding or oversown into existing swards (when plant numbers decline) / balanced stocking rate - grazed evenly and not out-competed by grass / clover friendly weed management plan

options: ensure adequate P and K levels
controlled nitrogen use (as this favours grass growth and suppresses clover)
rotational grazing – (use a tight grazing system) to prevent shading
avoid overgrazing in wet conditions or prevent poaching which damages clover
reseeding or oversown into existing swards (when plant numbers decline)
balanced stocking rate - grazed evenly and not out-competed by grass

questionText: Describe three stages of grass growth and identify the ideal growth stage for cutting.

rows.verbatim: Germination Stage: The radicle and plumule emerge / emergence of cotyledons / Leafy / Vegetative Stage: Grass is young with mainly leaf material (and little or no stem) / grass tillers / high in digestibility or energy or protein/ production of 3 leaves / Stem Elongation Stage: The stem begins to grow upwards (and the grass becomes less leafy) / fibre content increases /digestibility starts to fall / Reproductive / Heading / Flowering /inflorescence Stage: The seed head emerges / wind pollination occurs/ high fibre / low digestibility / Ideal Stage for Cutting: The best time to cut silage is during the leafy (vegetative) stage
rows.contextNote: Three described stages and the ideal cutting stage. The scheme prints 2(4)+2(1): the first two correct fields earn 4 marks each and the next two 1 each.

options: Germination Stage: The radicle and plumule emerge / emergence of cotyledons
Leafy / Vegetative Stage: Grass is young with mainly leaf material (and little or no stem) / grass tillers / high in digestibility or energy or protein/ production of 3 leaves
Stem Elongation Stage: The stem begins to grow upwards (and the grass becomes less leafy) / fibre content increases /digestibility starts to fall
Reproductive / Heading / Flowering /inflorescence Stage: The seed head emerges / wind pollination occurs/ high fibre / low digestibility
Ideal Stage for Cutting: The best time to cut silage is during the leafy (vegetative) stage

spray the field with pre-harvest or pre-emergence herbicides to reduce the weeds in the crop

stubble cleaning – depth of cultivation to target specific weeds
any valid qualified description of a point from diagram

rows.verbatim: Wear masks when spraying or wear gloves / take precaution when operating machinery / avoid drift / correct storage of chemicals

stem: Answer either (a) or (b).
questionText: Indicate if the following statements are true or false by place a tick (✓) in the correct box. The first one has been done as an example: Duration of heat in cattle is 48 hours — False. (i) The length of the oestrus cycle in cows is 17 days. (ii) Gestation length in cattle is 283 days. (iii) pH of the rumen is 7. (iv) Ideal Body Condition Score (BCS) for a cow at calving is 4.5. (v) The number of compartments in the ruminant stomach is 3.

rows.verbatim: (i) The length of the oestrus cycle in cows is 17 days — False
rows.contextNote: 2 marks for each statement (5(2)).

rows.verbatim: (ii) Gestation length in cattle is 283 days — True
(iii) pH of the rumen is 7 — True
(iv) Ideal Body Condition Score (BCS) for a cow at calving is 4.5 — False
(v) The number of compartments in the ruminant stomach is 3 — False

notes: Tariff 5(2) = five statements at 2 marks each = 10. The scheme prints only True/False against each roman numeral, so each row's verbatim is the single word and the statement it belongs to is carried in contextNote. The worked example on the paper (duration of heat in cattle is 48 hours) is not marked.

questionText: Farm animals are fed diets for maintenance and production. Explain the underlined terms.

rows.verbatim: Maintenance diet – amount of feed given to an animal to maintain good health or condition or with no loss or gain in weight
rows.contextNote: Maintenance diet – 1 mark.

rows.verbatim: Production diet – extra amount of feed required and used for production of some kind (1kg of LWG or 1 litre of milk or 1 kg of wool or produce calf or lamb)

notes: 1 mark for each of the two underlined terms. The scheme typesets the mark digit '1' inside the production-diet sentence, so the row quotes the head of the sentence (which carries the marking content, 'extra amount of feed') and the contextNote carries the tail. Both underlined terms appear in questionText, so no stem gloss is needed.

stem: Answer either (a) or (b). A student plants some seeds to investigate germination. In part (ii) you named one nutrient absorbed through the root.
questionText: A farmer discovers his crop is deficient in the nutrient named in (ii) above. Describe (1) a symptom and (2) the treatment for this deficiency.

rows.verbatim: Symptom — Spindly yellow plants or yellow leaves / leaves may have pink tints / stunted growth/ necrosis (death) of older leaves
rows.contextNote: Nitrogen: one symptom 2 marks and one treatment 2 marks.

rows.verbatim: Treatment — Spread chemical nitrogen (Urea or protected urea or CAN or named chemical compound e.g. 18‐6‐12) / spread slurry / spread FYM
Symptom — Spindly yellow plants or yellow leaves / leaves may have pink tints / stunted growth/ necrosis (death) of older leaves
rows.contextNote: Nitrogen: one symptom 2 marks and one treatment 2 marks.

rows.verbatim: Treatment — Spread chemical nitrogen (Urea or protected urea or CAN or named chemical compound e.g. 18‐6‐12) / spread slurry / spread FYM

Symptom — Reduced shoot growth / leaves turn dark or dull or blue‐green or pale in severe deficiency / reddish or reddish‐violet, or violet colour develops / lack of fruit or flowers/ wilting / delayed maturity
rows.contextNote: Phosphorus: one symptom 2 marks and one treatment 2 marks.

rows.verbatim: Treatment — Spread chemical phosphorus (named chemical compound e.g. 10‐10‐20 / spread FYM / spread slurry)
Symptom — Chlorosis (yellowing) at the leaf margins / reduced yield or slow growth / scorching of leaves / poorly developed root system / weak stalks
rows.contextNote: Potassium: one symptom 2 marks and one treatment 2 marks.

rows.verbatim: Treatment — Spread chemical potassium (potash) (named chemical compound e.g. 10‐10‐20 / spread FYM / spread slurry

Symptom — Plants are small and spindly / with short and slender stalks / stunted growth (prevent plants from utilising nitrogen) / maturity in cereals is delayed / nodulation in legumes may be poor or nitrogen‐fixation reduced / fruits often do not mature fully and remain light‐green in colour / chlorosis of leaves
rows.contextNote: Sulphur: one symptom 2 marks and one treatment 2 marks.

rows.verbatim: Treatment — Spread chemical sulphur (with fertiliser) / spreading slurry / spreading FYM

Symptom — Symptoms first appear on younger leaves and tissues / growth is inhibited / plants have a bushy appearance / youngest leaves are usually small or misshapen / brown chlorotic spots developing along the margins which spread to eventually unite in the centre of the leaves
rows.contextNote: Calcium: one symptom 2 marks and one treatment 2 marks.

rows.verbatim: Treatment — Adding lime (to soil in autumn) / apply a calcium supplement
Symptom — Chlorosis (yellowing of the leaves) or interveinal chlorosis (yellowing of the leaf with the veins remaining green) / reduced growth
rows.contextNote: Magnesium: one symptom 2 marks and one treatment 2 marks.

rows.verbatim: Treatment — Adding lime / apply a magnesium supplement

questionText: Describe two tests a farmer could do to assess the quality of the silage at the pit face.

questionText: Describe how any three of the following factors are involved in soil formation: Parent material, Topography, Time, Climate, Organisms.

rows.verbatim: Soil is formed by weathering of rock / mineral composition / texture or correct example of texture (coarse texture of granitic rocks leads to a coarse loamy soil texture) / pH of the soil is derived from the parent rock / Erosion will occur in steep slopes / thin layer of soil on hillsides / deep fertile soils in valleys / soils in valleys retain water (easy cultivation) / Over time, vegetation and climate act on parent material and topography / development determines a soil's age / the degree of aging depends on the intensity of the other four soil‐ forming factors / Temperature – heat and cooling of rocks (causing them to break) / low temperature leads to low water evaporation so more water for chemical weathering / precipitation – water contributes to physical or chemical weathering (freezing or solution or hydrolysis or hydration) / Provide humus when plant and animals die / microorganisms decompose organic matter (OM contributes to fertility and structure) / roots bind soil together / grasses contain alkaline compounds which reduce acidity in soil / acidic soils developed under forests / earthworms improve drainage or aeration or assist in soil formation
rows.contextNote: Any three of the five factors. The scheme prints 2+1+1: the first correct description earns 2 marks and the next two 1 each. In order the options describe parent material, topography, time, climate and organisms.

options: Soil is formed by weathering of rock / mineral composition / texture or correct example of texture (coarse texture of granitic rocks leads to a coarse loamy soil texture) / pH of the soil is derived from the parent rock
Erosion will occur in steep slopes / thin layer of soil on hillsides / deep fertile soils in valleys / soils in valleys retain water (easy cultivation)
Over time, vegetation and climate act on parent material and topography / development determines a soil's age / the degree of aging depends on the intensity of the other four soil‐ forming factors

Temperature – heat and cooling of rocks (causing them to break) / low temperature leads to low water evaporation so more water for chemical weathering / precipitation – water contributes to physical or chemical weathering (freezing or solution or hydrolysis or hydration)

Provide humus when plant and animals die / microorganisms decompose organic matter (OM contributes to fertility and structure) / roots bind soil together / grasses contain alkaline compounds which reduce acidity in soil / acidic soils developed under forests / earthworms improve drainage or aeration or assist in soil formation

stem: Read the article and answer the questions which follow. Robotics and Automation in Agriculture — The future of farming will likely be in automation, using robotic and self-driving machinery to sow, fertilise and harvest crops or manage animals. Already, automated or robotic milking machines are in use in Ireland and over 50% of all new milking machines installed in the European Union (EU) are automated. Robotic milking has a number of advantages. There is more consistency, reduced labour costs, the possibility of increased milking frequency (three times a day) and better overall herd management.
questionText: Outline two advantages of technology in agriculture.

rows.verbatim: Better use of chemicals / harvesting crops / sowing fertiliser (accurately) or saving fuel or saving fertiliser / reducing labour or time / more accurate data / increased animal yields / increased crop yield / better animal welfare / less leaching / tracking or monitoring animals or identification of disease or illness
rows.contextNote: Two advantages: the first correct earns 4 marks and the second 2 (4+2). The scheme adds "other valid answer".

options: sowing fertiliser (accurately) or saving fuel or saving fertiliser
tracking or monitoring animals or identification of disease or illness

stem: Question 15 is about making good quality grass silage on a beef farm. Part (c) reads: "The table below shows the analysis of the farmer's silage. Use these results to answer the questions which follow." The printed table gives, as farmer's analysis against target analysis - Dry Matter (DM): ? against 25%; Dry Matter Digestibility (DMD): 67% against 70% +; Crude protein: 12% against 15% +; pH: 4.7 against 3.8 to 4.2.
questionText: Outline two ways the farmer could have achieved the target pH during the production of the silage in line with the target analysis.

rows.verbatim: Cut at leafy stage to increase sugar for fermentation / do not cut during or after rainfall as water dilutes the sugar content / cut in the afternoon as photosynthesis produces more sugar / ensure pit (bales) packed tightly to remove air to promote growth of anaerobic bacteria (lactobacillus) / allow grass to wilt to increase sugar content / use additive (molasses or acid or inoculants) to achieve correct pH
rows.contextNote: Any 2: the first correct earns 4 and the next 2 (4+2). The scheme's own rule (PDF page 4): "the first correct answer encountered is awarded" the first mark, and each later correct answer the next.

options: Cut at leafy stage to increase sugar for fermentation
do not cut during or after rainfall as water dilutes the sugar content
cut in the afternoon as photosynthesis produces more sugar
ensure pit (bales) packed tightly to remove air to promote growth of anaerobic bacteria (lactobacillus)
allow grass to wilt to increase sugar content
use additive (molasses or acid or inoculants) to achieve correct pH

stem: Read the article and answer the questions that follow. NUTRIENT REQUIREMENTS OF BEEF CATTLE — Beef cattle productivity is highly dependent on nutrition and the ability of the animal's diet to meet nutrient requirements. To survive and be productive, beef cattle require water, energy, protein, minerals, and vitamins. (Adapted from mcdvetmanual.com) The amounts of nutrients that cattle require is influenced by various animal-related factors and environmental conditions.
questionText: State two animal-related factors or two environmental conditions.

rows.verbatim: Weight // age // sex // extent of production // composition // genetics // of physical activity // health // Temperature // humidity // chill or draught free // radiation or UV light // precipitation // soil nutrient deficiencies

notes: Tariff 2(2) = two answers at two marks each = 4, from a fourteen-item printed pool, so bestNofParts 2 of 14 @ 2. questionText is the paper's exact wording; the sentence that gives it its subject sits in the stem, so the card still stands alone. contextNote tags each row with the column it came from. The scheme prints this as a two-column table and the extraction interleaves the columns line by line, so five rows quote only the contiguous tail of their pool item and give the scheme's full wording in contextNote (r-4, r-5, r-7, r-11, r-12) — the same de-interleaving used elsewhere in this wave. No row is openList: the pool is now transcribed complete, and this scheme signals an open list explicitly when it means one (Q13(b)(ii) closes 'any named correct location'), which it does not do here.
